risk_of_fix: Lengthening the Abstract's already-dense final sentences could hurt readability; the authors may judge that the full caveat, preserved twice in the body (Introduction and Section 4), is sufficient and that the Abstract should stay maximally compressed. This is a legitimate compression-vs-completeness tradeoff for the authors to weigh.

location.section: Data and Experimental Context (main paper, p. 8-9)

issue: The paper reports that the 48 moderator variables required hand-coding of 'more than 100,000 data points' and that 'three of the co-authors collected 1/3 of the data each; another co-author randomly checked 1/3 of the entire dataset.' However, the manuscript provides no formal report of inter-coder reliability (e.g., Cohen's kappa, Krippendorff's alpha, or percentage agreement) between the three coders on any of the 48 variables. This is a standard methodological requirement for hand-coded data in systematic reviews (PRISMA guidelines).
why_it_matters: Without inter-coder reliability estimates, readers cannot assess the validity of the coding scheme or the magnitude of measurement error introduced into the meta-analysis. Coding errors in moderator variables inflate unexplained heterogeneity and can introduce spurious associations in the BMA results that follow. This is especially critical because the paper later uses BMA to filter 48 moderators down to 8 'robust' ones (PIP > 0.5)—if coding reliability is unknown, the PIP estimates may be distorted.
proposed_fix: Report inter-coder agreement statistics for the 48 moderator variables (pooled Cohen's kappa or Krippendorff's alpha for categorical variables; intraclass correlation for continuous ones). If only a subset of variables was tested for reliability, clearly state which ones and why. If disagreements were resolved by discussion (as the text suggests), report the frequency and nature of resolved disagreements and their distribution across moderators.
risk_of_fix: None. Reporting reliability estimates is a disclosure, not an edit that changes findings. If reliability is very low on some variables, the authors may need to exclude those moderators from BMA or weight them differently, but the paper should face that risk transparently.

logical-validity.reason: Lab 19% vs psychology 83% explicitly compared. Sample composition stated correctly.

location.section: Appendix A: Details of Literature Search (PRISMA flow diagrams, Figures A1-A3)

issue: The PRISMA flow diagrams (Figures A1-A3) report the number of studies excluded at the eligibility stage (163 for baseline, 318 for expanded, 281 for working papers) and reference 'a list of the [N] studies excluded at the eligibility stage (including reasons for exclusion), [available] in the online appendix.' However, this crucial transparency artifact is not displayed in the main paper or the submitted appendix text. The reasons for exclusion—critical for readers to assess whether inclusion criteria were applied consistently—are posted only to a URL (meta-analysis.cz/incentives), which is not archived in the submission and falls outside the scope of reproducible peer review.
why_it_matters: Transparency in study selection is a core PRISMA requirement. Post-hoc exclusion decisions made after reading full texts are a common source of selective reporting bias. Without seeing the reasons for the 163-318 exclusions, reviewers and readers cannot judge whether studies with 'inconvenient' results (e.g., large negative effects of incentives) were systematically excluded, or whether the inclusion/exclusion logic was applied consistently across studies.
proposed_fix: Include in the paper or appendix a summary table or list of the excluded studies and their reasons for exclusion, broken down by category (e.g., 'not an economics journal', 'no effect estimate or standard error reported', 'non-experimental design', 'missing data'). At minimum, report counts by reason. Alternatively, deposit the full list to a persistent repository (OSF, Zenodo, or the journal's data supplement) rather than a project website.
risk_of_fix: Modest pagination cost to add a summary table. Risk of revealing patterns in exclusions that might invite criticism, but the alternative—opaque exclusions—undermines the credibility of the meta-analysis entirely.

location.section: Appendix A: Details of Literature Search (Figure A1 notes)

quote: We screen the first 1,000 records retrieved from Google Scholar based on their relevance ranking.
issue: The baseline search (Figure A1) screens only the first 1,000 Google Scholar records. For the expanded dataset (Figure A2), because Google Scholar caps each search to 1,000 results, the authors report they 'split the search by publication year: before 2015 and 2015 or later.' This yields 2,000 screened records for expanded. However, the paper does not clarify whether additional year-splits were used for the working-paper search (Figure A3), which also screens 1,000 records. More critically, there is no justification for why 1,000 records is sufficient. If the search query is even moderately sensitive, studies at rank 1,001 onward could contain relevant papers missed by this cutoff.
why_it_matters: The screen-by-ranking strategy assumes Google Scholar's relevance ranking is reliable and that relevant papers cluster in the top 1,000. If the ranking algorithm is biased (e.g., favors highly-cited or recent papers), the selected studies may systematically miss small, contradictory, or methodologically novel experiments. This creates a form of selection bias distinct from publication bias: not all papers meeting inclusion criteria were even examined.
proposed_fix: Conduct a sensitivity analysis: screen a random sample of records ranked 1,001-2,000 (and for working papers, any available beyond 1,000) using the same inclusion/exclusion criteria. Report whether any of those records meet inclusion criteria, and if so, include them and re-run the main analyses. If none are found, report this as negative evidence that the 1,000-record threshold was adequate.
risk_of_fix: Moderate effort (scanning ~1,000 additional abstracts/titles). Risk of uncovering previously missed eligible studies that change the conclusions, but that is information the authors should have.

location.section: Data collection and coding description (main paper, p. 9)

issue: The paper collects 'the point estimate of the incentive-performance effect, the corresponding standard error, and the number of degrees of freedom used in the estimation.' However, there is no explicit statement of how ambiguous or multi-part estimates were handled. For instance: if a study reports both a main effect and a subgroup interaction (e.g., effect of incentives overall, and effect separately for high-ability vs. low-ability workers), which does the coder select as 'the' estimate? The roster notes that for '93% of the studies [they] collect multiple estimates, with an average of 25 estimates included per study' and that authors list 'various treatment arms,' 'subsample analyses,' and 'diverse estimation frameworks' as reasons for multiple estimates. But there is no codebook or decision tree provided to guide the selection of which estimates to include and in what priority order.
why_it_matters: Without an explicit, pre-registered prioritization rule for selecting among the multiple estimates per study, the coding becomes subjective and sensitive to author judgment. Coders might consistently prefer estimates that are statistically significant, or estimates from the authors' preferred specification, introducing selective-reporting bias within the included studies themselves. This compounds publication bias and undermines the assumption that the 2,193 estimates are a representative sample of underlying effect distributions.
proposed_fix: Publish a detailed codebook or decision tree showing: (1) the priority for selecting estimates if multiple are available (e.g., authors' preferred first, then main effect, then intent-to-treat, etc.); (2) rules for handling ambiguous cases (e.g., multiple treatment arms); (3) examples of how these rules were applied to 5-10 actual studies. Alternatively, if the authors collected *all* estimable effects and then weighted them post-hoc, report that design clearly and justify the weighting scheme.
risk_of_fix: Minimal. Publication of a codebook is a transparency enhancement, not a change to the findings (unless it reveals systematic bias in the prior selection, in which case the results should be corrected).

location.section: Data collection and coding (main paper, p. 9, and Table 3)

issue: For several moderator variables, the definitions in Table 3 rely on subjective judgment anchored to cited sources, with only thin operational guidance. Example: 'Task: appealing = 1 if the performed task is appealing to the subjects; defined following the authors of the primary studies and, when in doubt, following the standards used in psychology (Weibel et al., 2010).' This means that a task coded as 'appealing' is so coded because the primary study's authors said so, or because a coder judged it appealing by psychology standards. There is no explicit criterion (e.g., 'the paper says participants volunteered without pay', or 'the experimental design includes a stated intrinsic-motivation component'). Similarly, 'Motivation: altruism' is coded as '1 if the context of the experiment... is altruism', but without examples of what explicit study language would trigger a 1 vs. 0.
why_it_matters: Subjective coding rules with vague anchoring (e.g., 'when in doubt, use psychology standards') are a known source of coder drift, disagreement, and unreliability. If two coders independently read Charness & Gneezy (2009) on 'incentives to exercise,' one might code the task as 'appealing' (exercise is inherently fun) while another might code it as 'unappealing' (the study emphasizes extrinsic incentives). The single randomly-checked 1/3 of the dataset may have missed such drift in the unchecked 2/3.
proposed_fix: Provide operational definitions for the subjective variables (appealing, crowding-out theory, altruism, reciprocity, fairness) that include: (a) explicit, measurable criteria from the text (e.g., for altruism: 'coded 1 if the paper explicitly mentions helping others or charitable outcomes; coded 0 otherwise'); (b) 3-5 concrete worked examples (e.g., 'Frey & Oberholzer-Gee (1997) on nuclear-waste disposal = altruism because...'; 'Shearer (2004) on tree-planting = money only because...'). Post-hoc, ask the three data collectors to independently code 20 test cases and report pairwise kappas to demonstrate the reliabilty of the operational definitions.
risk_of_fix: Minimal. Providing operational definitions is a disclosure that may reveal past coding inconsistencies (in which case those should be corrected), but improves future transparency and replicability.

location.section: Data collection and coding (main paper, p. 9)

quote: Three of the co-authors collected 1/3 of the data each; another co-author randomly checked 1/3 of the entire dataset.
issue: The random-check strategy is described as one co-author checking 1/3 of the entire dataset. However, there is no clarity on: (1) whether the checks were blind (did the checker know whose subset they were checking?); (2) what 'checking' entailed (full re-reading of the paper, spot-checks of 1-2 entries per study, or complete re-coding of all moderators?); (3) the threshold for discrepancies (were all disagreements logged, or only 'significant' ones?); (4) whether the checker was independent of the three primary coders (i.e., not one of them, and not aware of their coding choices?). The phrase 'discovered inconsistencies were discussed among the co-authors and corrected for the entire dataset' suggests that disagreements were resolved by consensus, which can reintroduce bias if the group shares a common view of a contested variable.
why_it_matters: The validity of the check rests on its design. If the checker was not blind, knew the coder's prior choice, or resolved conflicts by majority vote rather than by reference to the codebook, the check may have corrected obvious errors but missed systematic bias. A well-designed check (blind, full re-coding of a random subset, with discrepancies resolved by reference to an operationalized codebook, not by discussion) can substantially improve confidence in the data quality.
proposed_fix: Report: (a) whether the checker was blind to the coders' prior entries; (b) the exact procedure for the check (e.g., 're-coded all 48 moderators for each of the [N] checked studies'); (c) the frequency and distribution of discrepancies found (e.g., 'of [N] moderators checked, [X]% had at least one discrepancy, [Y]% had discrepancies corrected'); (d) the rule used to resolve discrepancies (e.g., 'all disagreements were resolved by re-consulting the primary paper and the codebook; consensus was used only after codebook rules were applied'). If feasible, report pairwise Cohen's kappas for the primary coders vs. the checker on a representative subset.
risk_of_fix: Minimal. This is a methodological disclosure. If checks reveal systematic errors in one coder's subset, the authors may need to flag which studies were coded by that coder and whether conclusions are robust to excluding that subset—but that is important information.

quote: We show that the experimental evidence in economics does not support this view unconditionally.
issue: This paper dies the way every meta-analysis dies that lets its abstract say more than its design can license: it tells readers 'increasing financial rewards rarely produces large performance gains' while admitting in its own next breath that the literature it pooled was assembled by researchers who 'rarely conduct experiments in contexts where incentives are expected to have large... effects... because such results are considered trivial' — so the paper spends 40 pages precisely estimating the average size of an effect in a sample explicitly curated to exclude the cases where that effect would be large, and then states the resulting near-zero average as if it were evidence about effect size in general.
proposed_fix: Either (a) rewrite the abstract and introduction's headline sentences to carry the same scope qualifier that appears in Section 3 ('within the kinds of contexts researchers have chosen to study'), making the limitation visible at first contact, or (b) explicitly model/bound how much the design-stage selection could move the estimated mean, so the 'rarely produces large gains' claim is something other than an artifact of the sampling frame.
risk_of_fix: Softening the headline to match the caveat will make the contribution sound less decisive and could itself read as an admission that the paper cannot answer the question its title and abstract pose — a real cost to the paper's marketability that the authors will resist.

logical-validity.reason: Direct quote: 'design-stage selection...cannot be corrected in a meta-analysis.' Logically sound.

location.section: Introduction, p.6 (paragraph beginning 'A related limitation, which can be viewed as another form of publication bias...')

quote: Researchers rarely conduct experiments in contexts where incentives are expected to have large and obvious effects (for example, comparing one dollar to one thousand dollars for a routine task) because such results are considered trivial.
issue: The authors name the fatal confound themselves, in plain language, and then proceed as though naming it discharges the obligation to address it.
proposed_fix: At minimum, attempt a directional argument: is there reason to think design-stage selection biases the corrected mean up, down, or is agnostic? Even a qualitative bound ('if anything this selection should bias our estimate toward zero/away from zero, because...') would let the headline stand on firmer ground than bare acknowledgment.
risk_of_fix: Any directional claim about an unobservable selection process is itself speculative and could be challenged as another unfounded assertion — possibly creating a second front for attack rather than closing the first.

logical-validity.reason: Winsorizing at 1% stated; non-winsorized results in Tables B6-B7. Accurately described.

location.section: Section 2 (Data and Experimental Context), p.9, formula (1)

quote: We thus recompute them to partial correlation coefficients (PCCs) according to the following formula:
issue: The single number that everything in the paper is built on — the partial correlation coefficient — is manufactured by collapsing wildly different statistical objects (OLS coefficients, logit/probit marginal effects, DID estimates, RCT treatment effects measured in grades, dollars, counts, and binary outcomes) through one formula keyed only on a t-statistic and degrees of freedom, and the paper never demonstrates that this transformation preserves a comparable construct across that diversity.
proposed_fix: Report PCC distributions stratified by estimation technique (OLS vs. logit vs. probit vs. DID, etc.) before any pooling, and show — or argue from theory — that the resulting scale is comparable across techniques; alternatively restrict the headline analysis to a methodologically homogeneous subsample and treat the rest as robustness.
risk_of_fix: Stratifying by method could shrink usable cell sizes to the point that the headline 'lab + loss framing' result, already resting on roughly a fifth of the sample, becomes statistically indistinguishable from noise — undermining the very headline the fix was meant to shore up.

logical-validity.reason: Quote: '93% of studies...multiple estimates, with an average of 25 per study.' Directly supported.

quote: This procedure yields 396 preferred and 856 non-preferred estimates for the baseline dataset.
issue: The paper builds an entire 'preferred vs. non-preferred' classification — a variable that the paper's own Bayesian model averaging then tests as a moderator of the headline effect — by having the authors themselves judge, estimate by estimate, which results the ORIGINAL authors 'favored', without ever reporting an inter-coder agreement statistic for that judgment call.
proposed_fix: Report an explicit inter-coder reliability statistic for the 'preferred estimate' classification specifically, ideally from an independent, blinded second coding of a random subsample.
risk_of_fix: If the reliability statistic comes back low, the authors would be forced either to drop a variable that is currently load-bearing for the headline Table 5 computation, or to re-code the entire sample — a costly outcome the fix itself would have surfaced.

location.section: Introduction, p.3 (paragraph beginning 'Figure 1 presents a bird's-eye view...')

quote: However, laboratory experiments on this topic are relatively rare in economics, comprising only 19% of the estimates.
issue: The paper's only positive, statistically significant, headline-worthy finding — the lab-plus-loss-framing effect — is built almost entirely on the rarest cell in the data, and the paper says so in the same breath it reports the result.
proposed_fix: Report the lab-times-loss-framing cell's raw N, perform an explicit power analysis for that interaction, and either downgrade its prominence in the abstract to match its fragility or gather additional lab-plus-loss-framing estimates before headlining it.
risk_of_fix: If a power analysis shows the cell is underpowered (plausible, given ~19% x ~9% of 1,252 implies on the order of dozens of estimates from a handful of studies), the paper loses its only positive finding and is left with a purely null result — a much harder sell at a top field journal.

logical-validity.reason: Partial correlation standardization explained due to varying performance metrics. Logically motivated.

location.section: Section 2 (Data and Experimental Context), p.11 — the paragraph describing the coding process ('Three of the co-authors collected 1/3 of the data each; another co-author randomly checked 1/3 of the entire dataset. The discovered inconsistencies in coding were discussed among the co-authors and corrected for the entire dataset.')

issue: The paper describes its hand-coding quality-control process in terms that sound rigorous but never report the one number that would let a reader judge whether it actually was: an inter-coder reliability statistic for the 100,000+ hand-entered data points.
proposed_fix: Report the number/rate of discovered coding inconsistencies from the 1/3 check, and ideally compute and report a formal inter-coder agreement statistic on an independently double-coded random subsample of the full 88-study set.
risk_of_fix: Computing this after the fact requires returning to original sources and re-coding a subsample independently — a substantial cost that could also, if the resulting statistic is unflattering, force re-analysis of Section 4's heterogeneity results.

quote: We thank Anna Dreber and Uri Gneezy for comments that helped us improve the paper substantially.
issue: The acknowledgments thank two named scholars — one of whom (Uri Gneezy) is the author or co-author of at least four of the 88 primary studies the meta-analysis itself codes, scores, and in several places singles out by name as illustrative examples — for comments that 'helped... improve the paper substantially,' without the paper anywhere disclosing or discussing this dual role as both commentator-on and subject-of the analysis.
proposed_fix: Add a short disclosure noting which acknowledged commentators (or referees) are authors of primary studies in the sample, and confirm that their estimates were coded by co-authors blind to that overlap (or explain why blinding was not feasible).
risk_of_fix: An explicit disclosure could itself draw more attention to the relationship than the current silence does, and might invite scrutiny of every other primary-study author the team may have consulted informally but not named.

location.section: Introduction, p.3 (paragraph beginning 'Figure 1 presents a bird's-eye view...')

quote: This estimate lies on the threshold between a negligible and small effect according to the guidelines by Doucouliagos (2011).
issue: The paper's headline positive finding is reported as sitting precisely on a threshold the authors themselves chose as their interpretive yardstick — and then is narrated, in the abstract and introduction, in language ('statistically significant', 'small but significant positive effects') that reads as more decisive than 'on the threshold between negligible and small' actually is.
proposed_fix: Add 'borderline' or equivalent qualifying language to the abstract's description of the lab/loss-framing finding, mirroring the careful 'on the threshold' language used in the body.
risk_of_fix: A more hedged abstract reduces the paper's only quotable positive finding to something less citable — a real cost in a literature that rewards crisp headline numbers.

location.section: Introduction, p.3 (end of paragraph beginning 'Figure 1 presents a bird's-eye view...')

quote: Only three studies overlap between our meta-analysis and that of Kim et al. (2022).
issue: The paper reports, almost in passing, that its sample overlaps with its chief psychology rival (Kim et al., 2022) in only three studies — a number that, if foregrounded rather than buried, would by itself raise the question of whether the paper is comparing two literatures or two largely disjoint samples dressed up as a disciplinary contrast.
proposed_fix: Either drop the compositional-reweighting explanation for the Kim et al. discrepancy, or explicitly justify why near-zero study overlap does not undermine treating the two analyses as comparable slices of one underlying literature.
risk_of_fix: Removing the Kim et al. comparison weakens one of the paper's central rhetorical contrasts (the economics-vs-psychology divide that motivates the whole project), leaving the introduction's framing thinner.

location.section: Introduction, p.5 (paragraph beginning 'A solution is to use the inverse of the square root...')

quote: Such an instrument is correlated with the standard error by the definition of the latter and can be expected to be less related to method choices.
issue: The instrument the authors prefer above all other bias-correction techniques — and adopt as 'preferred' on the strength of a single specification test — is defended with an assertion about its exclusion properties that is never independently tested against the very confound (method choices) the paper itself says creates the endogeneity problem in the first place.
proposed_fix: Report an overidentification or falsification test of the MAIVE instrument's exclusion restriction specific to this sample — e.g., test whether the instrument correlates with the 35 BMA moderators after conditioning on the standard error, or run MAIVE separately within method-homogeneous subsamples and compare.
risk_of_fix: If such a test reveals correlation between the instrument and method-choice moderators, the paper's preferred correction technique — and its preferred headline corrected-mean number — would need to be replaced, likely with a less favorable (less precise, or less negligible) estimate from one of the rival techniques in Table 2.

logical-validity.reason: Relies on table-specific values. Cannot verify exact numbers from text extraction.

location.section: Introduction, p.5 (paragraph beginning 'Our initial identification assumptions are based on the Lombard effect...')

quote: It is telling that only half of the studies in our sample mention motivation crowding theory.
issue: A throwaway parenthetical is asked to do real argumentative work it cannot support: the fact that only half the sampled studies mention motivation-crowding theory is offered as evidence that economists hold a prior belief in incentives' effectiveness — but a study not mentioning a psychological theory says nothing about what its authors believe about incentive effectiveness, only about which theoretical frameworks they cited.
proposed_fix: Either drop the sentence, or replace 'It is telling that' with a more measured framing such as 'Consistent with this, we note that only half of the studies in our sample explicitly engage with motivation crowding theory, though this is at best indirect evidence of researchers' prior beliefs.'
risk_of_fix: Minimal — this is a low-cost, low-risk wording fix with no entanglement in any numerical result.

location.section: Appendix A, Figure A1 (PRISMA flow diagram for the baseline dataset), p.40

quote: Studies excluded due to lack of correspondence or data (n = 163)
issue: 163 studies were excluded from the baseline sample for 'lack of correspondence or data' — a number nearly three times the size of the final included sample (54) — and the paper never reports whether these exclusions are random with respect to the reported effect, leaving open the possibility that an entire tier of studies with non-corresponding authors or unavailable data systematically differs in effect size or direction from the studies that made it in.
proposed_fix: Compare observable metadata (publication outlet, year, citation counts, abstract-reported direction of effect where available) between the 163 excluded-for-non-response studies and the 54 included studies, to bound whether this attrition stage plausibly differs systematically from random.
risk_of_fix: Such a comparison could itself reveal a directional pattern (e.g., excluded studies skew toward null or negative abstract-reported findings), which would hand critics a second, harder-to-rebut selection story layered on top of the publication-bias correction the paper already performs.

location.section: Title-page footnote (p.1, corresponding-author note); repeated near-verbatim at pp.11, 21, 30

quote: Data and code are available in an online appendix at meta-analysis.cz/incentives.
issue: The paper repeatedly promises that 'data and code are available,' but nowhere in the manuscript does it specify a license, a persistent archival mechanism (e.g., a DOI-backed repository such as Zenodo or OSF), or a commitment to maintain the linked website beyond the authors' own institutional lifespans — leaving the paper's central replicability claim resting entirely on a single self-hosted URL.
proposed_fix: Deposit the dataset and code in a third-party archival repository with a persistent DOI (e.g., Zenodo, OSF, or a journal-affiliated data repository), and cite that DOI alongside (or instead of) the institutional URL.
risk_of_fix: Essentially none — this is a low-cost infrastructural addition with no entanglement in the paper's substantive claims.

quote: Our results suggest that increasing financial rewards rarely produces large performance gains in the experimental settings most studied by economists.
issue: The abstract frames the headline conclusion as a general claim about what happens in 'experimental settings' without mentioning that these settings are themselves curated to exclude obvious incentive-effect contexts. The readers is not cued to the major design-stage-selection caveat that narrowly scopes the study's applicability until page 70 of the introduction. This positioning creates overclaiming on external validity.
why_it_matters: Policy makers and practitioners reading only the abstract or title will believe the finding generalizes to most laboratory and field experiments on incentives, not realizing that the entire experimental literature has deliberately avoided running high-power tests where effects would be obvious. This scope condition fundamentally changes the interpretation of the findings.
proposed_fix: Revise abstract to read: 'Our results suggest that increasing financial rewards rarely produces large performance gains in the experimental settings that economists have chosen to study — notably, settings that tend to avoid contexts where incentive effects are expected to be obvious.' Or add a brief qualifier like 'in most contexts economists have studied'.
risk_of_fix: Longer abstract; minor. However, the current wording is not technically false, just under-qualified, so the fix is editorial in nature rather than a correction of fact.

logical-validity.reason: Quote: 'Few estimates exceed 0.33, a threshold denoting large estimates.' Visually confirmed in Figure 2.

quote: Researchers rarely conduct experiments in contexts where incentives are expected to have large and obvious effects (for example, comparing one dollar to one thousand dollars for a routine task) because such results are considered trivial. Instead, experimental designs often focus on boundary cases where incentives might backfire or interact with other motives, precisely because such findings are more interesting to publish.
issue: This critical scope condition appears on page 70 (late in the Introduction) and is explicitly framed as a design-stage selection that 'cannot be corrected in a meta-analysis'. Yet the paper's abstract and repeated policy-facing conclusions ('rarely produces large performance gains', 'financial incentives improve performance' phrasing) do not explicitly signal this limitation. The design caveat is buried rather than prominently integrated into the headline claim.
why_it_matters: The literature selection mechanism fundamentally inverts the generalizability of the findings. If true large-effect contexts are deliberately avoided, the near-zero mean reported here may be exactly what should be expected and tells us almost nothing about how incentives perform in real labor markets or organizations where such contexts are common. This is not a minor methodological note but a scope condition that could flip the policy interpretation.
proposed_fix: Restructure the narrative: (1) Lead with the design-stage-selection finding upfront in the Introduction before the empirical results, not as an afterthought. (2) Make the scope condition explicit in the abstract or a subheading immediately after it. (3) Ensure every policy-facing statement ('rarely produces', 'little evidence') is directly paired with the qualifier about which contexts the finding applies to.
risk_of_fix: None. This is a narrative/framing change that makes the paper's own logic more transparent without altering any statistical claims.

logical-validity.reason: Quote: 'most studies report both positive and negative estimates' and mean close to zero for older studies. Directly quoted.

quote: In any case, we find it premature to proclaim that experimental research shows, without qualification, that financial incentives improve performance. Yet such proclamations are common in the practical use of experimental evidence.
issue: The conclusion critiques practitioners and policymakers for making overconfident claims about incentives, but uses hedging language ('premature to proclaim', 'without qualification') that obscures the real problem: the literature has self-selected away from the very contexts where large effects are theoretically and practically most likely. The paper then pivots to discussion of 'alignment' and 'task characteristics' without re-anchoring these points to the scope limitation. A reader might conclude the paper is cautioning against overgeneralization in general, not identifying a specific and severe selection mechanism.
why_it_matters: The criticism of McKinsey/CIPD statements (lines 18-19, 1362) is warranted but incomplete. The paper should explicitly note that its own findings do not refute those claims — they are silent on them — because the experiments were never designed to test those claims. Failing to make this connection could lead readers to overinterpret the paper's refutation of industry practice.
proposed_fix: Add to the conclusion: 'A caveat: our findings are largely silent on the practical claims made by consultancies and HR professionals, because the experimental literature has deliberately avoided the high-powered, real-world incentive comparisons those claims would require. Our results argue for skepticism about large unconditional effects in the studied contexts, but they do not test (and thus cannot refute) whether generous incentives improve performance in labor markets or organizations.'
risk_of_fix: Strengthens honesty and scope clarity without changing any findings. Minor risk: might weaken the paper's policy impact if readers interpret it as making no contribution to the consultant/CIPD debate, but this is actually more truthful.

issue: The paper states the design-stage selection caveat but does not explicitly quantify or characterize how severe the selection is. For example, it does not say: 'The field has avoided X% of the theoretically relevant incentive-comparison space' or 'Only Y studies/estimates involve the extreme comparisons (e.g., $1 vs. $1000) that would most clearly test the consultancy claim.' This leaves the reader without a metric for how much of the problem space the meta-analysis actually covers.
why_it_matters: A reader trying to assess the external validity cannot judge severity without knowing the size of the gap. If 99% of the theoretically relevant contexts are excluded, the finding is mostly about a nonrepresentative tail; if 20% are excluded, it is a modest limitation. The paper's silence on quantification weakens the reader's ability to properly scope the conclusion.
proposed_fix: In the Introduction or early Results section, estimate or report: (1) How many studies in the initial search explicitly test high-stakes/high-power incentive comparisons and were excluded? (2) What is the threshold incentive magnitude above which the literature drops off? (3) Survey the 54 studies for whether any explicitly justify design choices to avoid 'trivial' effect sizes and count them. Report this denominator to give scope bounds.
risk_of_fix: Requires additional analysis or at minimum a literature survey of justifications in the 54 studies. Moderate effort. Could reveal that the authors have little direct evidence of design-stage selection and must rely on inference—which is fine to admit but changes the claim's standing.

location.sentence_range: Abstract line 7, Intro lines 70, Conclusion lines 1361, 1363

quote: Our results suggest that increasing financial rewards rarely produces large performance gains in the experimental settings most studied by economists.
issue: The jump from 'corrected mean near zero' to 'rarely produces large performance gains' uses policy-relevant language that may overstate the scope claim, given that the paper's own design-stage-selection caveat (line 70) admits the literature was never designed to measure large incentive effects in the first place. A steelmanship reading notes the word 'rarely' is a proper hedge, but the framing elides the distinction between 'we found no large effects in a self-selected literature' and 'large effects rarely occur'—which are different claims.
why_it_matters: The most likely use of this paper by policymakers is to conclude that financial incentives are not worth implementing at scale. But if the underlying literature avoids exactly the high-stakes contexts where incentives are most powerful, the policy claim 'rarely produces large gains' cannot be separated from the methodological scope limitation without reader confusion.
proposed_fix: Explicitly state in the abstract or headline conclusion: 'we find no large effects in the subset of experimental contexts that economists have chosen to study, which tend to avoid high-stakes, obvious-outcome scenarios. We cannot conclude from our data whether large effects are rare in contexts we do not observe.'
risk_of_fix: The proposed fix makes the paper's policy message much weaker and less actionable for practitioners. The authors may argue the current framing is already sufficiently hedged by 'in the experimental settings most studied.' The fix also slightly shifts emphasis from the main result (near-zero corrected effect) to a caveat (design-stage selection), potentially diluting the headline.

quote: A key insight from the literature is that incentives do not operate in isolation: they interact with task characteristics, intrinsic motivation, and social norms.
issue: This statement—which is core to the paper's careful framing—is presented as 'a key insight from the literature,' but it is not clear whether the paper itself provides evidence for this claim or merely observes that heterogeneity across contexts exists. The claim moves from what the data shows (near-zero average, heterogeneous by lab/field) to a causal mechanism (interaction with task characteristics, intrinsic motivation, norms) without explicitly testing those mechanisms. A steelmanship reading accepts this as a literature synthesis claim rather than an original causal finding, but the phrase 'from the literature' is vague and could be misread as an empirical finding the paper itself establishes.
why_it_matters: If readers treat 'incentives interact with task characteristics' as an empirical finding of THIS paper, they may overstate the specificity and directedness of the paper's guidance. The paper's actual contribution is to report heterogeneity (lab vs. field, framing effects) and to cite existing literature on possible mechanisms, not to identify the mechanisms themselves.
proposed_fix: Clarify: 'Recent literature suggests incentives operate in context-dependent ways (e.g., Rusz et al. 2020 on distraction). Our heterogeneity findings—differences in lab vs. field, positive framing effects—are consistent with such mechanisms, though our data do not directly test them.'
risk_of_fix: Minimal. This is a presentational clarification that strengthens the paper's intellectual honesty without weakening its main results.

issue: The paper's design-stage-selection caveat ('Researchers rarely conduct experiments in contexts where incentives are expected to have large and obvious effects ... This design-stage selection narrows the scope of the available evidence and cannot be corrected in a meta-analysis,' stated at line 70 in the Introduction) is not explicitly revisited in the Conclusion. A reader skimming from Abstract to Conclusion may internalize the policy message 'financial rewards rarely produce large gains' without fully grasping that this claim is bounded by a literature that deliberately avoids testing those gains. The paper's framing is careful, but its emphasis structure—placing this key limitation deep in Section 1 rather than returning to it in the Conclusion—creates a risk of misreading even a cautiously-phrased paper.
why_it_matters: Under steelmanship, the paper IS careful; but careful writing requires not just qualifying language but also structural emphasis. A well-crafted steelman version would emphasize (not demote) its most important boundary condition.
proposed_fix: Return to the design-stage-selection limitation explicitly in the Conclusion: 'Our headline finding—that financial incentives produce near-zero effects in typical economics experiments—must be read in light of the fact that such experiments are rarely conducted in high-stakes, obvious-payoff scenarios where large effects would be expected. Our results constrain claims about the experimental margin economists study; they do not adjudicate whether incentives matter in real-world labor markets with much larger stakes.'
risk_of_fix: Minimal. This reiterates a limitation the authors already acknowledge; it only adjusts emphasis and placement for maximum impact on the reader.

quote: In any case, we find it premature to proclaim that experimental research shows, without qualification, that financial incentives improve performance.
issue: The paper offers multiple candidate explanations for the near-zero finding (distraction, measurement error, limited power, design-stage selection), but does not establish which is most plausible or likely. This is intellectually honest in avoiding overcommitment, but it also blunts the paper's own claim. The phrase 'In any case' signals that the authors are not themselves wedded to a single mechanism, which is admirable for a steelman framing but may leave readers unsure what the paper's verdict actually is. Is the message 'incentives don't work' or 'we can't tell because of low power / measurement error'? Both are stated, and their relative importance is left ambiguous.
why_it_matters: A steelmanship reading appreciates the multi-mechanism humility, but it also notes that this ambiguity—while honest—makes the paper's actionable guidance less clear. Policymakers seeking direction will find three different stories (distraction, power, measurement error) without guidance on which to prioritize.
proposed_fix: Add a brief paragraph weighing the relative plausibility of the three mechanisms: (1) Our finding that lab experiments (where distraction cues are more controlled) show larger effects supports the distraction hypothesis. (2) Limited power is a possible but less satisfying explanation, since we employ large meta-analytic samples. (3) Design-stage selection is the most important boundary—this is a correctable limitation of future experimental design, not a limitation of the paper's evidence. We thus emphasize this last point as our primary scope limitation.
risk_of_fix: The authors may resist picking a 'winner' among explanations, viewing this as editorializing. But the fix actually strengthens their steelmanship by grounding each explanation in evidence and ranking them by the paper's own data.

quote: While our results may appear discouraging from the perspective of standard economic theory, they offer guidance for designing incentive schemes more effectively.
issue: The paper's Conclusion claims its results 'offer guidance for designing incentive schemes more effectively.' But what guidance? The paper identifies that lab experiments show a small positive effect (0.07 PCC) and that loss framing helps, but it does not offer prescriptive design principles. The claim 'they offer guidance' is aspirational and goes beyond what the data supports. A careful steelman acknowledges the authors then provide examples (framing, alignment, intrinsic motivation support), but these are not derived from the paper's own analysis—they are cited from the literature (Fryer et al., Ariely et al., Gneezy & Rustichini) or merely asserted as plausible implications.
why_it_matters: Under strict steelmanship, the paper should claim only what it shows: near-zero effects on average, heterogeneity by context, and consistency with multiple explanatory mechanisms. The leap to 'offers guidance for designing' is a framing overreach that conflates literature synthesis with the paper's own empirical contributions.
proposed_fix: Revise: 'Our findings constrain the scope of unconditional claims about incentives' universality, but actionable guidance for practitioners requires more work. The heterogeneous effects we identify—particularly the lab/loss-framing exception and the distraction-effect hypothesis—suggest that future research should test whether high-stakes, carefully-framed incentive schemes in applied settings produce larger effects than those observed in typical experiments.'
risk_of_fix: This makes the paper sound less prescriptive and more tentative, which may reduce its appeal to practitioners and policymakers. However, it is more honest about what the data can and cannot claim.

quote: Our results suggest that increasing financial rewards rarely produces large performance gains in the experimental settings most studied by economists.
issue: The abstract and title foreground a confident, policy-relevant claim ('rarely produces large gains') but the manuscript then reveals in the design-stage selection passage (line 70) that the experimental literature itself is non-randomly selected: researchers avoid 'contexts where incentives are expected to have large and obvious effects...because such results are considered trivial.' This means the 'rarely' claim applies only to experiments designed NOT to find large effects. The authors acknowledge this is 'uncorrectable' in a meta-analysis, yet the policy-forward framing in the abstract persists without proportional qualification.
why_it_matters: A reader or policymaker seeing the abstract might conclude 'the evidence shows rewards rarely help.' But the evidence is actually: 'among experiments designed to study boundary cases, modest stakes, and interesting task-incentive interactions, rewards show near-zero effects.' These are radically different claims. The first generalizes to the real world; the second is methodologically honest but much narrower. Foregrounding the narrow claim as a broad policy statement is a fatal overclaim because it reverses the evidential hierarchy (what the literature has chosen to study is presented as what the literature has found about incentives).
proposed_fix: Revise abstract to make the scope-limitation explicit in the headline claim. Example: 'Our results suggest that in the experimental settings economists have chosen to study—typically boundary cases with modest stakes—increasing financial rewards rarely produces large performance gains.' Alternatively, downgrade the policy language and lead with the narrower, methodologically honest finding: 'the corrected mean effect across the studied experiments is close to zero.'
risk_of_fix: If the abstract is revised to include scope caveats, the paper loses some of its apparent practical relevance and may be seen as more methodological/specialist. The authors may feel the scope limitation is already disclosed on line 70. However, that disclosure comes after the headline claim, which violates clarity-first principles.

logical-validity.reason: Motivation crowding discussed in Section 1; contrasted with distraction effect. Contextual application addressed.

quote: Our findings are not fully consistent with the motivation crowding theory, as the effect of incentives appears similarly small for both interesting and uninteresting tasks.
issue: The claim that results are 'not fully consistent with motivation crowding theory because effects look similar for interesting and uninteresting tasks' is a misrepresentation of the theory. Motivation-crowding theory (Deci et al., 1971; Frey & Jegen, 2001) predicts crowding out (negative effects) for intrinsically interesting tasks but not for purely instrumental tasks. It does NOT predict that effects must be different across task types; rather, it predicts that the MECHANISM differs (crowding in interesting tasks, no crowding in boring tasks). Finding near-zero effects for both is consistent with: (a) crowding in interesting tasks being offset by effort increases, or (b) crowding being masked by measurement error, or (c) the distraction effect (which the authors themselves propose). It is NOT inconsistent with the theory. The authors mischaracterize the theory to claim novelty in showing near-zero effects across task types.
why_it_matters: By claiming to be a neutral adjudicator ('our results do not fit neatly...either'), the authors implicitly claim high credibility on the fundamental question of whether incentives help or hurt. But the framing here obscures that a near-zero corrected effect, taken at face value, is closer to the psychology prediction than the economics one. The mischaracterization of motivation-crowding theory (saying near-zero effects show the theory is wrong when near-zero is compatible with the theory if crowding is offset) undermines the intellectual honesty of the psychology-economics dialogue the paper purports to advance.
proposed_fix: Acknowledge that the near-zero result is actually more consistent with motivation-crowding concerns than with the 'incentives reliably help' economist prior. Clarify: 'We do not find evidence that incentives reliably improve performance, which aligns with psychologists' caution about motivation crowding and task-context interactions. However, we also do not find large negative effects, which might suggest crowding is often offset by other mechanisms (e.g., effort increases) or is context-dependent in ways the data cannot fully resolve.'
risk_of_fix: This revision softens the paper's claimed novelty as a 'bridge' between fields. It may also invite criticism that the authors are now closer to the psychology side than they originally claimed. However, it would be more honest about what the corrected near-zero effect actually means.

logical-validity.reason: Quote: '48 contextual factors' and 'fill more than 100,000 data points by hand.' Directly stated.

location.sentence_range: Throughout; notably absent from Abstract and Conclusion discussion of policy implications

issue: The paper does not formally address whether the 'design-stage selection' caveat materially undermines or even reverses the policy relevance of the central finding. The authors write (line 70): 'This design-stage selection narrows the scope of the available evidence and cannot be corrected in a meta-analysis.' They then conclude (line 1356-1361) with policy-forward language: 'we find it premature to proclaim...that financial incentives improve performance' and cite a McKinsey quote. But they never explicitly state: 'Given that our literature is non-randomly selected to exclude high-stakes, non-boundary-case contexts, our evidence on those contexts is almost absent. Therefore, we cannot actually conclude what happens when firms implement high-stakes incentives in routine tasks—the very contexts where practitioners most care about effects.' This silence is a fatal framing flaw because it allows readers to misinterpret the scope of the conclusion.
why_it_matters: A policymaker might read the conclusion as: 'incentives rarely help' (global claim), when the honest interpretation is: 'among the niche contexts economists have studied, incentives show near-zero effects, but this tells us little about the real-world high-stakes cases.' The absence of an explicit, upfront statement of what the evidence CAN'T address is a critical silence that allows the policy claim to float free of its methodological moorings.
proposed_fix: Add to the Conclusion a paragraph like: 'An important limitation of our findings is that they apply to the experimental margin economists have chosen to investigate. Because researchers avoid trivial contexts (large incentive differences on routine tasks), our meta-analysis contains little evidence on the efficacy of high-powered incentives in labor markets or routine organizational tasks. Our findings therefore caution against assuming incentives 'always help,' but they do not justify the opposite claim—that incentives rarely help in real-world, high-stakes settings. The gap between our studied contexts and practitioner contexts remains a frontier for future research.'
risk_of_fix: This revision reduces the apparent boldness of the policy claim. The authors may resist it if they view the design-stage selection discussion on line 70 as sufficient. However, placing it only in a footnote or in the middle of the introduction is not sufficient disclosure for a paper that leads with policy language.

logical-validity.reason: Quote: 'negative framing...typically leads to larger reported effects.' Consistent with loss aversion theory.

quote: Our findings are not fully consistent with the motivation crowding theory, as the effect of incentives appears similarly small for both interesting and uninteresting tasks.
issue: This claim misrepresents motivation-crowding theory. The theory (Deci et al., 1971; Frey & Jegen, 2001) predicts that intrinsic-motivation crowding occurs for tasks that are intrinsically interesting, but not for purely instrumental tasks. The prediction is NOT 'effects differ between task types' but rather 'crowding out is task-dependent'—meaning a negative effect for interesting tasks (crowding) and weaker or zero effect for boring tasks. A near-zero effect for BOTH task types is compatible with this prediction if: (a) the boring-task category also has small positive effects (from pure extrinsic motivation) that offset measurement error, or (b) crowding occurs but is offset by other mechanisms. The authors offer 'distraction effect' as an alternative explanation, which is fine, but claiming the near-zero result CONTRADICTS motivation-crowding theory is unsupported.
why_it_matters: By falsely claiming the theory is contradicted, the authors present their result as more novel or surprising than it is. In fact, a careful reading of motivation-crowding theory would predict near-zero or small heterogeneous effects once publication bias is corrected. The authors' mischaracterization inflates the appearance of a theory-shaking finding and weakens the intellectual integrity of the psychology-economics dialogue.
proposed_fix: Revise to: 'Our findings provide limited support for task-specific crowding effects as predicted by motivation-crowding theory. We observe small effects for both interesting and uninteresting tasks, which could reflect either a failure of the theory to apply in this experimental context, or the theory's predictions being masked by offsetting mechanisms (e.g., effort increases, distraction effects) or measurement issues. These alternatives warrant further investigation.'
risk_of_fix: This softens the claim that the paper 'bridges' or 'challenges' motivation-crowding theory. It may make the paper appear less novel. However, it is more intellectually honest.

logical-validity.reason: Multiple techniques employed (linear, nonlinear, endogeneity-robust) all yield small effects. All cited; results in Table 2.

location.sentence_range: Introduction cites McKinsey quote as a foil; Abstract claims to refute it

quote: Generous and specific financial incentives can help drive and sustain a rapid performance improvement. (McKinsey, 2022)
issue: The paper opens by citing McKinsey's claim that incentives 'can help drive and sustain rapid performance improvement' as a representative view to be tested. The authors then claim to refute it with their near-zero finding. However, McKinsey's claim is carefully hedged with 'can help'—a probabilistic statement, not 'always help.' The authors' finding that incentives 'rarely' (not 'never') help is not actually a contradiction. Furthermore, the paper finds that lab+loss-framing does yield 0.07 effects, which in practice might constitute 'help' for a manager (though borderline negligible). The paper thus sets up a straw-man version of the McKinsey position and then refutes a stronger claim than McKinsey actually made.
why_it_matters: This softens the credibility of the paper's framing. If the paper is claiming to challenge overstated practitioner belief, it should be precise about which claims are being challenged. Quoting 'incentives can help' and then saying 'they rarely help' is not a clear contradiction—both could be true if 'can help' means 'sometimes do' and 'rarely' means 'in most of our studied contexts.'
proposed_fix: Either (a) find a stronger quote from practitioner literature that actually claims incentives 'always help' or 'reliably improve performance,' or (b) rephrase the paper's conclusion as: 'Our findings suggest that in the specific experimental contexts economists have studied, incentives show near-zero effects in most field settings, with modest but statistically significant effects in laboratory settings. This qualifies the optimistic view, represented by industry practitioners, that incentives universally drive performance improvement.'
risk_of_fix: This revision might weaken the rhetorical force of the paper's opening salvo against practitioner overconfidence. However, it would be more logically defensible.

quote: We find that positive framing tends to be associated with smaller estimates, which is consistent with loss aversion.
issue: The paper grounds the loss-framing heterogeneity finding in a pre-existing behavioral theory (loss aversion) rather than presenting it as a post-hoc discovery. This is a theoretically motivated finding.
why_it_matters: Establishing theoretical grounding is the primary defense against post-hoc fishing charges. Loss aversion is a foundational economic theory, and the authors explicitly invoked it before analyzing the moderators.

quote: A potential explanation is that reward cues distract people from the task itself. A recent meta-analysis in psychology shows that this effect can be important (Rusz et al., 2020): people focus on the rewards instead of the work. The distraction effect can be present for both interesting and uninteresting tasks and is more likely in field settings, where the experimenters do not always have full control over the connection between reward cues and the task itself. The distraction effect can thus be associated with our finding that lab experiments tend to yield more evidence for the effect of financial incentives on performance.
issue: The paper provides an explicit, testable theory-based explanation for lab-vs-field heterogeneity grounded in independent meta-analytic evidence (Rusz et al. 2020). This is not left as unsupported narrative.
why_it_matters: Heterogeneity findings are strongest when accompanied by mechanistic explanations. The distraction effect theory offers a behavioral pathway distinct from publication bias or confounding.

quote: Only 8 variables have posterior inclusion probabilities above 0.5, which means that most of the variables are not useful for the explanation of the differences in the reported incentive-performance effects.
issue: The BMA approach imposed a 0.5 PIP threshold, which is a principled, pre-specified standard in Bayesian literature (Eicher et al. 2011, Steel 2020). The authors did not tune this threshold post hoc.
why_it_matters: This demonstrates methodological discipline: heterogeneity variables were subject to a formal, conservative inclusion filter. Lab and loss-framing variables that emerge survive a legitimately strict standard.

quote: Table 4 also reports the results of frequentist model averaging, which has the benefit of clustering standard errors at the study level. Four of variables with inclusion probabilities above 0.5 are not significant at the 5% level. That leaves 4 variables that are robustly associated with the reported estimates of the incentive-performance nexus.
issue: The finding converges across two independent model-averaging approaches: Bayesian (dilution prior) and frequentist (Mallow's weights + orthogonalization + study-level clustering). Multi-method convergence is a hallmark of robustness.
why_it_matters: If the lab/loss finding were a Bayesian artifact, it would not survive frequentist analysis with study-level clustering. Cross-method agreement strengthens the defense against fragility claims.

quote: As additional robustness checks, in the Appendix (Table B12) we provide two adjusted versions of our baseline Bayesian model averaging exercise. First, we use different priors: the BRIC g-prior based on Fernandez et al. (2001) and the beta-binomial model prior according to Ley & Steel (2009).
issue: The authors tested robustness to alternative priors (BRIC, beta-binomial) and weighting schemes, with honest caveats about which results are fragile. This is transparency rather than selective reporting.
why_it_matters: Full disclosure of specification dependence is a sign of methodological integrity. The authors flag that framing loses robustness in one specification, showing they are not hiding inconvenient results.

quote: This estimate lies on the threshold between a negligible and small effect according to the guidelines by Doucouliagos (2011). However, laboratory experiments on this topic are relatively rare in economics, comprising only 19% of the estimates.
issue: The authors explicitly flag the 0.07 finding as borderline (at the negligible/small threshold per Doucouliagos 2011) and note the lab subsample represents only 19% of data. This is honest framing rather than overselling.
why_it_matters: Authors understate rather than oversell their heterogeneity finding: calling it borderline, noting its threshold status, and acknowledging the small subsample. This preempts overclaiming and shows epistemic humility.

quote: To address these issues, we distinguish between two groups of estimates: (i) those the authors themselves appear to favor, and (ii) all others. This classification serves as a proxy for methodological and data quality considerations that are otherwise challenging to formalize.
issue: The preferred/non-preferred classification is defensible: it uses author emphasis (abstract, intro, conclusion) as a quality proxy, consistent with Lang (2025) and Opatrny et al. (2025). This is principled and replicable.
why_it_matters: The heterogeneity analysis includes both preferred and non-preferred estimates. Robustness across both subsets demonstrates the finding is not driven by low-quality studies, strengthening the defense.

quote: Only 8 variables have posterior inclusion probabilities above 0.5, which means that most of the variables are not useful for the explanation of the differences in the reported incentive-performance effects. Table 4 also reports the results of frequentist model averaging, which has the benefit of clustering standard errors at the study level. Four of variables with inclusion probabilities above 0.5 are not significant at the 5% level.
issue: The lab+loss framing result (PCC = 0.07, cited as the paper's 'only exception' to negligible effects) is not a directly estimated interaction coefficient. Instead, it is a fitted value computed by additive combination of separate marginal effects (Laboratory experiment = 0.052, Negative framing = -0.039) in Table 4. No interaction term was explicitly estimated, and the framing variable's posterior inclusion probability falls below 0.5 in at least one robustness specification (Table B12), making the foundation of this headline finding fragile.
why_it_matters: The entire paper hinges on the claim that lab + loss framing is a 'borderline exception' (0.07, 'on the threshold between negligible and small'). If this result is not robust to modest changes in priors (as Table B12 shows) and was never explicitly tested as an interaction, the paper's central positive finding evaporates, leaving only 'close to zero' across all contexts. This shifts the contribution from 'there is one exception' to 'there are no exceptions,' materially changing the policy and theoretical interpretation.
proposed_fix: Explicitly estimate an interaction term between Lab and Negative Framing in the BMA framework (or frequentist model averaging) and report its posterior inclusion probability, coefficient, and confidence interval separately. If the PIP is below 0.5 or the interaction is not robustly positive, the headline claim must be revised from 'lab + loss is an exception' to 'we find no robust exceptions.'
risk_of_fix: The fix requires re-running the BMA/model-averaging pipeline with a new interaction variable, which may reveal that the interaction term is weakly included or negative. The authors may also discover that the lab and framing marginal effects, when combined additively under BMA, do not actually yield the reported 0.07 after controlling for all the nuances of model averaging. The result could confirm the fragility rather than the robustness of the finding.

logical-validity.reason: Explicitly distinguishes preferred/non-preferred and documents justifications. Procedure clearly stated.

quote: test of the Andrews-Kasy model, shown in Table B10 in the Appendix, suggests that in our case estimates are indeed correlated with standard errors even in the absence of publication bias, we prefer the MAIVE approach
issue: Table B10 shows that the correlation between the log absolute value of estimates and log standard error, after MAIVE reweighting by inverse Andrews-Kasy publication probabilities, is 0.647 [0.567, 0.668] for baseline, and 0.458 [0.352, 0.564] for preferred estimates. Both confidence intervals exclude zero. The authors cite this test as *diagnosing a violation* of the Andrews-Kasy model's assumptions (uncorrelation in the absence of bias) and then use this diagnosis as justification to switch to MAIVE. However, this is circular: the test shows MAIVE does not eliminate the correlation, yet MAIVE is still chosen as the 'preferred' method. The foundation of the corrected effect (0.03–0.07) rests on an instrument (inverse sqrt degrees of freedom) that may be correlated with study design and unobservable method choices, violating the exclusion restriction.
why_it_matters: The central quantitative claim—that the corrected mean effect is 'close to zero'—depends critically on the choice of MAIVE over other methods (Andrews-Kasy, p-uniform*, linear meta-regression). Table B10's diagnosis of persistent correlation post-MAIVE suggests that the instrument is not exogenous. If the exclusion restriction fails (inverse sqrt df correlates with true effect through method-design choices), the MAIVE estimates are biased and the paper's bottom-line conclusion is unreliable.
proposed_fix: Report the complete set of corrected estimates from all methods (Table 2 Panels A–C) side-by-side in the main paper, not just the appendix. Explain why MAIVE is preferred despite the continued correlation shown in Table B10 (e.g., by arguing that some correlation is expected even if the instrument is valid). Alternatively, investigate the relationship between sqrt(df) and study design variables (task type, population, year) to test the exclusion restriction. If significant associations emerge, the MAIVE estimate should be de-emphasized or sensitivity-tested.
risk_of_fix: If the authors transparently report that MAIVE's corrected effect is not substantially different from linear meta-regression or Andrews-Kasy, they may reduce confidence in the method choice. Conversely, if a sensitivity analysis reveals that the exclusion restriction is violated, the corrected effect may be larger or smaller than reported, and the paper's headline will be less certain.

logical-validity.reason: Figure B3 and Table B1 show jump at t=0 but not significance thresholds. Quote: 'p-hacking...selection for intuitive sign.'

quote: Our main results hold, but in one specification the inclusion probability for the positive framing variable falls below 0.5.
issue: The paper reports that when BMA is re-run with alternative priors (BRIC g-prior, beta-binomial) or alternative weights (inverse variance + inverse number of estimates per study), the posterior inclusion probability for 'Positive framing' (i.e., negative framing when flipped) drops below 0.5. Since the lab+loss result is computed from the combination of Lab (PIP=1.0) and Negative Framing (PIP=0.958 in baseline), the robustness check reveals that framing's inclusion is fragile. The brief sentence in the main text downplays this fragility by saying 'main results hold,' but if framing drops out, the 0.07 lab+loss cell in Table 5 is no longer supported by robust model-averaging consensus.
why_it_matters: The paper's only positive finding (0.07 in lab+loss setting) is presented as robust and consensus-based ('borderline exception'). Yet the appendix robustness check shows that the framing variable—one of the two essential components—is not robustly included. This directly contradicts the narrative that the lab+loss result is a solid empirical finding. If framing is omitted, the fitted value would collapse back toward the lab-only effect (0.073) or the overall mean (0.031).
proposed_fix: Investigate which prior/weighting choice causes the framing PIP to fall below 0.5 and report the resulting 0.07 estimate (or its replacement) in Table B12 for that specification. If the 0.07 disappears or shrinks substantially, revise the abstract, introduction, and conclusion to reflect that the lab+loss finding is not robust across all reasonable prior and weighting schemes. Alternatively, provide a principled argument for why the baseline prior is the canonical one and robustness failures should be downweighted.
risk_of_fix: A full transparency assessment may reveal that the 0.07 finding is an artifact of prior choice. The fix could require substantially revising the paper's headline claim. However, the transparency itself strengthens the paper's credibility and guards against overstatement.

logical-validity.reason: Quote: 'researchers rarely conduct experiments...where incentives...have large effects...Instead...boundary cases.' Directly quoted.

quote: The very best model includes 8 variables out of 35. The sum of posterior model probabilities for all the models in which the corresponding variable is included gives rise to posterior inclusion probability for each variable
issue: The BMA operates over >30 billion possible models, searching through a space where 35 variables can be included or excluded. Only the 8 variables with highest posterior model probability are likely to be visited frequently by the MCMC algorithm. This creates a risk of model-selection bias: if the true model includes framing and lab effects, but the MCMC undersamples the region where this combination appears (e.g., because those models fit slightly worse on mean-squared error than models that omit one variable), the posterior inclusion probability for framing may be artificially depressed. The paper does not report MCMC convergence diagnostics, the number of chains, or the number of iterations walked, making it impossible to assess whether the inclusion probabilities are trustworthy.
why_it_matters: If the MCMC algorithm did not adequately explore the model space (e.g., due to poor mixing or insufficient burn-in), the reported posterior inclusion probabilities are artifacts of the sampler, not true Bayesian summaries. The fragility of framing's PIP (it drops below 0.5 in Table B12) may be a sign that MCMC did not converge. Without diagnostics, readers cannot judge whether the 0.07 lab+loss finding is a genuine Bayesian consensus or a computational artifact.
proposed_fix: Report Gelman-Rubin convergence diagnostics (Rhat), effective sample size (ESS), autocorrelation, and trace plots for the main BMA run. Confirm that Rhat < 1.01 for the posterior inclusion probabilities of Lab and Negative Framing. If MCMC diagnostics show poor mixing, re-run with longer chains or different starting values. Report the total number of MCMC iterations, burn-in, and thinning.
risk_of_fix: MCMC diagnostics may reveal poor convergence, requiring longer computation or algorithm redesign. However, proper diagnostics are necessary for credibility. If convergence is confirmed, it strengthens confidence in the results; if it is not, it indicates a need for remediation.

logical-validity.reason: Quote: 'field experiments...dominating...help explain why...psychology...finds positive mean effect.' Composition noted.

issue: The paper does not report a formal test of the lab × negative framing interaction. Instead, it reports the marginal effects separately and computes a fitted value combining them additively (Table 5). No coefficient, standard error, confidence interval, or posterior inclusion probability is provided for the interaction term. This is a critical omission: if the interaction is not explicitly modeled and tested, the finding that lab+loss yields 0.07 is merely a constructed prediction based on additivity, not an estimated effect with known uncertainty.
why_it_matters: Interactions are notoriously fragile in meta-analysis when not explicitly modeled. The paper's claim that lab+loss is an 'exception' rests on post-hoc computation of a fitted value, not a pre-specified or directly estimated interaction. This is a textbook example of specification search and data dredging: among 35 variables and >30 billion combinations, the authors found that two variables (lab, negative framing) happen to point in the same direction, and they combined them to create a headline result. A proper heterogeneity analysis would include interactions as explicit terms in the model.
proposed_fix: Add an explicit interaction term Lab × Negative Framing to the BMA model. Report its posterior mean, standard deviation, and posterior inclusion probability in Table 4 (or a new table). Compute Table 5's fitted values using the interaction coefficient, not additively. If the interaction term has PIP < 0.5 or includes zero in its credible interval, the lab+loss 'exception' claim must be qualified or withdrawn.
risk_of_fix: The interaction may not be included in high-probability models, or may even be negative. The headline finding of a lab+loss exception would vanish, fundamentally changing the paper's conclusion. However, this is a risk only because the finding is fragile; the fix itself is methodologically sound.

logical-validity.reason: Applies Doucouliagos (2011) thresholds (0.07=negligible, 0.17=small, 0.33=large). Correctly used per guidelines.

quote: We collect 2,193 estimates from 88 economics experiments and account for 48 contextual fac-tors. Using recent advances in correcting for publication bias and p-hacking, we find that the corrected mean effect of financial incentives on performance is close to zero across most field contexts. Laboratory settings and loss framing yield statistically significant but mod-est positive effects even after bias correction.
issue: The abstract claims that lab settings and loss framing yield 'statistically significant' effects. However, Table 5 shows the 95% confidence interval for the combination (Negative framing cell) is [0.001, 0.131], which includes values very close to zero. The lower bound of 0.001 is not meaningfully distinguishable from zero in any practical sense. The paper hedges this later by calling it a 'borderline exception,' but the abstract's use of 'statistically significant' overstates the certainty and strength of this finding.
why_it_matters: Readers relying on the abstract will believe that lab+loss effects are 'statistically significant.' This is not supported by the confidence interval, which is nearly consistent with zero. The framing in the abstract is more assertive than the evidence warrants and may mislead practitioners or policymakers into overweighting a fragile, marginal finding.
proposed_fix: Revise the abstract to say 'Laboratory settings and loss framing yield modest positive effects in the 'best practice' specification (PCC = 0.07), but this finding is borderline and sensitive to model specification (Table B12); confidence intervals include values near zero.' Or: 'We find no statistically significant effects in most contexts after bias correction, with only a borderline positive effect for lab experiments combined with negative framing.'
risk_of_fix: A more cautious abstract may reduce the paper's apparent impact. However, it more honestly reflects the data.

quote: Our results suggest little evidence that financial incentives improve performance in experiments unconditionally. We also fail to find evidence that increasing reward size proportionally boosts performance.
issue: The paper's central interpretive move is to claim that the near-zero corrected effect means 'incentives don't improve performance.' However, as the authors acknowledge in Section 1 and the Conclusion (Section 5), researchers deliberately avoid designing experiments in 'contexts where incentives are expected to have large and obvious effects' because such results are considered trivial. This design-stage selection cannot be corrected in a meta-analysis. Given this, the paper is analyzing an intentionally restricted sample of 'boundary cases' and 'interesting' effects. To claim 'incentives rarely produce large gains' when the literature was designed to avoid testing large gains is logically inconsistent. The paper's policy conclusion—that 'poorly designed incentives may yield little benefit'—is warranted; but the stronger claim that 'incentives themselves are ineffective in experimental settings' overstates the scope of the evidence.
why_it_matters: The paper's policy relevance rests on the claim that practitioners should not expect large effects from incentives. However, if the experimental literature intentionally focuses on edge cases and boundary conditions, the absence of large effects in that literature does not imply that incentives are ineffective in general. This is a fundamental scope error that undermines the paper's headline conclusion, even if the statistical analysis of the literature is sound. Practitioners reading the paper may wrongly conclude that incentives are ineffective across all contexts, when the paper's evidence only covers a narrow slice of the design space.
proposed_fix: Revise the abstract and conclusion to explicitly state: 'Our findings apply to the subset of experimental designs that researchers have chosen to investigate. Because this subset deliberately avoids obvious incentive scenarios (as the authors themselves acknowledge), our finding of near-zero effects should not be interpreted as evidence that incentives are universally ineffective. Instead, our results suggest that in the types of experiments economists have designed—which often test boundary cases and psychological effects—financial incentives have modest, context-dependent impacts.' Emphasize that the paper describes the literature as it is, not incentives as they work in all real-world contexts.
risk_of_fix: A narrower scope statement reduces the policy-relevance claim and may diminish the perceived contribution. However, it is necessary for intellectual honesty and prevents misapplication of the findings.

logical-validity.reason: Quote: 'Weibel et al. (2010)...none of the psychology meta-analyses correct for publication bias.' Accurate.
