location.section: 1 Introduction / 3 Publication Bias / Table 2 notes (and Tables B4, B6, B7, B9, B12 notes)

quote: use the inverse of the square root of the number of degrees of freedom as an instrument for the standard error
issue: The paper defines its preferred bias-correction instrument (MAIVE) inconsistently. In the body text it is described twice as 'the inverse of the square root of the number of degrees of freedom' (Introduction: 'A solution is to use the inverse of the square root of the number of degrees of freedom as an instrument for the standard error (Irsova et al., 2025)'; Section 3: 'One solution to these problems is to use the inverse of the square root of the number of degrees of freedom as an instrument for the standard error (MAIVE, Havranek et al., 2024; Irsova et al., 2025)'). But every table note describing the same MAIVE specification (Table 2 and the structurally identical notes reproduced for Tables B4, B6, B7, B9, B12) instead states 'MAIVE = a linear version of the meta-analysis instrumental variable estimator due to Irsova et al. (2025), in which we use the inverse of the square root of the number of observations as an instrument for the standard error.' Degrees of freedom (df = N - k, where k is the number of estimated parameters) and the number of observations (N) are not interchangeable, and the paper's own PCC formula (equation 1) treats t and df as the operative quantities, not N. Because MAIVE is explicitly chosen as the 'preferred' correction technique on which the headline near-zero corrected effect rests, a reader (or replicator) cannot tell from the manuscript which variable was actually used to build the instrument.
why_it_matters: MAIVE is singled out as the preferred bias-correction estimator and its 'almost identical' results across specifications are repeatedly invoked to defend the headline near-zero corrected effect (e.g., 'with our preferred MAIVE model giving almost identical results'). An instrument defined on the number of observations versus one defined on degrees of freedom can have materially different correlation properties with the standard error and with method-choice confounders (the very 'unobserved heterogeneity' channel the authors invoke to motivate using an instrument at all), so the choice is not cosmetic -- it is the crux of the instrument's claimed exogeneity. A referee who notices the contradiction cannot verify that the instrument used in the reported tables matches the one motivated and defended in the prose, undermining confidence in the single most load-bearing correction in the paper.
proposed_fix: Pick the correct definition (most likely 'degrees of freedom', consistent with the prose motivation and with Irsova et al. 2025/Havranek et al. 2024) and make every table note (Table 2 and its B4/B6/B7/B9/B12 reproductions) match it verbatim; alternatively, if 'number of observations' is in fact what was coded and run, correct the two body-text passages (Introduction and Section 3) to match and re-justify the instrument's exogeneity properties accordingly, since the argument given ('correlated with the standard error by definition... less related to method choices') was built around degrees of freedom.
risk_of_fix: If the authors discover the actual code uses one definition but the cited source (Irsova et al., 2025/MAIVE) uses the other, harmonizing the prose to the code could require re-deriving or re-stating the instrument's exogeneity argument, which is more than a copy-edit; conversely, blindly editing the table notes to match the prose without checking the code risks creating a textual consistency that papers over a real coding discrepancy.

logical-validity.reason: Assumptions explicit: no correlation absent bias and linear function of SE. Both stated in text.

quote: The Bayesian approach, however, treats all observations as independent, and to account for within-study dependence we also employ frequentist model averaging with Mallow's weights (Hansen, 2007) and orthogonalization of model space according to Amini & Parmeter (2012).
issue: The authors themselves flag that their baseline Bayesian model averaging (BMA) -- run on 1,252 estimates of which 93% come from multi-estimate studies averaging 25 estimates each -- 'treats all observations as independent,' a direct violation of the dependence structure the paper elsewhere insists must be handled by study-level clustering ('The standard errors of the regression parameters are clustered at the study level and shown in parentheses'). Yet the paper's headline heterogeneity outputs -- the posterior inclusion probabilities in Table 4/Figure 6 (e.g., PIP = 1 for the standard error, the lab and framing variables singled out in the abstract) and the Table 5 'implied incentive-performance effect for different contexts' (the basis for the headline 0.03 'best-practice' mean, C-052) -- are explicitly constructed 'using the results of Bayesian model averaging' (the independence-violating exercise), with the dependence-aware frequentist model averaging relegated to supplying only confidence intervals as a secondary cross-check ('Approximate 95% confidence intervals constructed using frequentist model averaging are reported in the last two columns').
why_it_matters: This is an internal inconsistency in the paper's own evidentiary standard: clustering at the study level is treated as a non-negotiable requirement everywhere else in the paper (Table 1, Table 2, Tables B4-B9, the PCC meta-regression), but the central moderator-selection exercise that produces the paper's signature numbers (the 0.03 best-practice mean, the PIP=1 claims, the lab+loss-framing exception) runs on a method the authors concede does not respect that same dependence structure. Pointing to the frequentist robustness check does not resolve this, because the headline point estimates (Table 5, the implied-context numbers) are taken from the Bayesian exercise, not the frequentist one -- so the 'fix' for dependence is applied to the uncertainty bands but not to the point estimates that anchor the paper's central claims.
proposed_fix: Either (a) construct the headline Table 5 implied-context estimates (and the posterior-inclusion-probability ranking that motivates which moderators are 'robust') from the dependence-aware frequentist model-averaging exercise (or from a Bayesian procedure that itself accounts for clustering, e.g., via study-level aggregation or a hierarchical prior) and present the current BMA run as the robustness check instead, or (b) explicitly quantify and report how much the Table 5 point estimates and the PIP rankings move when within-study dependence is respected, so the reader can judge whether the acknowledged independence violation is consequential for the headline numbers rather than only for their confidence intervals.
risk_of_fix: Re-deriving Table 5 from the frequentist exercise (or a clustering-aware Bayesian one) could change the headline 0.03 number and the set of moderators crossing the 0.5 inclusion-probability threshold -- precisely the numbers the abstract and conclusion are built around -- so this is a substantive re-run, not a cosmetic correction, and the authors may reasonably resist it without first checking whether the two approaches in fact converge (as the paper currently asserts they roughly do for the four 'robust' variables).

logical-validity.reason: All techniques cited: Ioannidis et al., Andrews & Kasy, Bom & Rachinger, Furukawa. Employed; results shown.

quote: Fifty-four studies satisfy our inclusion criteria; we will call them primary studies.
issue: While walking through the inclusion criteria (economics journals, English language, reportable standard errors and degrees of freedom), the paper states that 'Fifty-four studies satisfy our inclusion criteria; we will call them primary studies' -- but every other count of the analyzed sample in the manuscript (the abstract's '2,193 estimates from 88 economics experiments,' the later 'In total, in this meta-analysis we consider 88 studies shown in Table A1,' Table A1's title '88 studies included in the meta-analysis,' and the comparison to Brown et al. and Matousek et al. 'covering 88 primary studies and 2,193 estimates') says 88. No definition is given anywhere that would let 54 and 88 both be correct counts of two different, clearly-labeled subsets (the 54-vs-88 gap is not explained by the later-introduced 'expanded' (69) or 'working paper' (19) subsets, since 54 + 19 = 73 ≠ 88, and 54 is smaller than the 69-study expanded count it should logically precede).
why_it_matters: This is a basic numerical inconsistency about the size of the very dataset the meta-analysis is built on -- the kind of 'correctness/integrity error' the rubric treats as potentially capping the headline verdict on its own. A referee encountering '54' immediately after the inclusion-criteria description and before the 88-study count will reasonably wonder whether an intermediate sample-construction step (e.g., before snowballing, before working papers, or a stale draft figure) was left in by mistake, and whether the funnel from search to final sample (Figure A1's PRISMA diagram) is internally consistent with both numbers.
proposed_fix: Either replace 'Fifty-four' with '88' if it is a leftover from an earlier draft of the sample-construction narrative, or, if 54 genuinely denotes an intermediate count (e.g., studies meeting the baseline Google Scholar search criteria before snowballing/working-paper additions), state explicitly what that intermediate count represents and how it reconciles arithmetically with the final 88 (and with the PRISMA flow diagrams in Figures A1-A3), so the funnel from search to final sample is auditable end to end.
risk_of_fix: If '54' actually reflects a genuine, distinct stage of the sample-construction pipeline that the authors simply forgot to label, a careless global find-and-replace to '88' would erase a true and useful intermediate statistic and could even mask a real funnel-arithmetic problem worth surfacing rather than hiding.

location.section: 2 Data and Experimental Context / 3 Publication Bias

issue: The paper states 'We winsorize the effects at the 1% level to limit the influence of outliers' immediately after introducing the PCC transformation and its formula ('Using the computed partial correlation and the original t-statistic we then obtain the corresponding standard error of the standardized measure (Stanley & Doucouliagos, 2012)'), but never says (a) whether winsorizing is applied to the PCC, to the underlying t-statistic/point estimate before the PCC transform, or to both PCC and Cohen's d in the expanded dataset; (b) whether the standard error of the winsorized PCC is recomputed from the winsorized value or still derived from the original (pre-winsorizing) t-statistic via the Stanley & Doucouliagos formula referenced in the same breath; and (c) how winsorizing at the 1% level interacts with bias-correction techniques that are explicitly tail-sensitive by design -- Top10 (uses only the most precise 10% of estimates), the stem-based method (endogenously trades off bias and variance at the tails), the endogenous-kink model (defines a 'highly statistically significant' segment), and the Andrews-Kasy selection model (models publication probability as a step function of significance thresholds). Each of these techniques' behavior could plausibly be sensitive to whether the 1% trimming was performed before or after the PCC/SE pairing was fixed, yet the chain from 'raw estimate -> winsorize -> PCC -> SE -> bias-correction battery' is never made fully explicit.
why_it_matters: Winsorizing changes the joint distribution of (estimate, standard error) pairs that the entire publication-bias battery is built on, and several of the chosen nonlinear techniques are explicitly tail- or threshold-based. If winsorizing is applied to the PCC but the paired standard error is left as derived from the unwinsorized t-statistic (or vice versa), the estimate-SE pairing that identifies publication bias (the Lombard-effect logic the paper leans on -- 'studies with a large standard error will need a large point estimate to overcome noise') would be internally inconsistent for the 1% of winsorized observations, which is exactly the part of the distribution these tail-sensitive techniques weight most heavily. The robustness check the paper does report (Table B6: 'we lose statistical significance in some specifications' without winsorizing) is consistent with winsorizing mattering for some techniques -- which makes the missing description of exactly how it was implemented more, not less, consequential.
proposed_fix: Add one or two sentences specifying precisely which variable(s) are winsorized (PCC only, Cohen's d only, both, and/or the underlying t-statistics/point estimates pre-transformation), whether the paired standard error is recomputed consistently with the winsorized value, and whether winsorizing is applied separately within the baseline, expanded, and working-paper subsamples or on the pooled distribution -- ideally cross-referenced to the publicly posted code so a referee or replicator can confirm the implementation matches the description.
risk_of_fix: None of substance -- this is a clarification of an already-performed step, not a re-analysis; the only risk is that, once specified precisely, the implementation might turn out to be inconsistent with the bias-correction logic described elsewhere, which would itself be worth knowing rather than concealing.

location.section: Table 2 notes / Tables B4, B6, B7, B9, B12 notes (boilerplate methods glossary)

quote: Study = weighted by the inverse of the number of estimates reported per study, Precision = weighted by the inverse of the estimate's standard error
issue: Minor notes folded into one item: (i) the identical multi-paragraph methods glossary in the notes to Table 2 is reproduced verbatim across at least seven tables (B4, B6, B7, B9, plus the Cohen's-d variants), which is exactly the kind of copy-paste boilerplate that let the MAIVE 'degrees of freedom' vs. 'number of observations' inconsistency (S-METHODS-AUDITOR-F1) propagate silently into every reproduction rather than being caught once; (ii) the claim that 'different weights do not change the conclusion, and any systematic differences seem to be small' (Table 1 discussion) is asserted qualitatively without a pointer to where a reader could see the weighted-vs-unweighted comparison quantified beyond the two summary columns of Table 1 itself; (iii) the phrase 'we had to fill more than 100,000 data points by hand after reading the primary studies' together with 'another co-author randomly checked 1/3 of the entire dataset' leaves unstated what error rate that spot-check found, which would let a reader gauge how much to trust the hand-coded moderators that the entire heterogeneity and BMA analysis (Section 4) is built on.
why_it_matters: None of these three individually changes a conclusion, but together they are the kind of presentation friction that makes the 'end-to-end methodological coherence' this seat is charged with auditing harder to verify by inspection -- a reader has to manually cross-check seven near-identical table notes for silent drift, cannot locate the quantitative basis for the 'weights don't matter' claim, and cannot assess the reliability of the hand-coded moderator data from the description given.
proposed_fix: Centralize the repeated methods glossary into a single cross-referenced footnote or appendix subsection (reducing the surface area for copy-paste drift like F1); add a one-line pointer to the specific table/figure (or appendix table) where the weighted-vs-unweighted comparison across the bias-correction battery is shown quantitatively; and report the inter-coder error rate (e.g., 'X% of the spot-checked 1/3 required correction') found during the co-author cross-check of the hand-coded moderators.

location.section: 1 Introduction / Table 5 (Effects implied for different contexts)

issue: The paper reports a single point estimate and one 95% CI for the headline 'lab + loss framing' exception (PCC = 0.07, CI (0.01, 0.14)) and explicitly says this value 'lies on the threshold between a negligible and small effect.' But nowhere does the paper report a power/precision analysis for this specific cell -- e.g., how many of the 2,193 (or 1,252 baseline) estimates actually fall jointly into 'laboratory' AND 'loss framing' (a sub-sub-sample of the already-rare 19% lab estimates), what the implied minimum detectable effect is for that cell, or how sensitive the 0.07 figure is to the inclusion/exclusion of a handful of studies. Given that the entire paper's one positive finding rests on this borderline cell, the absence of any stated cell size, design-based power calculation, or precision discussion for it is a load-bearing gap: a reader cannot tell whether (0.01, 0.14) reflects a well-powered estimate of a real small effect or a thinly-populated cell whose CI happens to exclude zero.
why_it_matters: Per the rubric, 'no power analysis behind a null' (or, symmetrically, behind the one non-null finding the paper foregrounds) is a canonical missing load-bearing analysis. The lab+loss-framing result is the single piece of positive evidence the abstract, introduction, and conclusion all lean on to avoid a fully null headline ('Laboratory settings and loss framing yield statistically significant but modest positive effects even after bias correction'). If that cell is thinly populated, the CI's exclusion of zero could be an artifact of a small, noisy subgroup rather than a robust discovery -- which would mean the paper's only non-null claim, and therefore a chunk of its contribution, rests on an unreported precision basis.
proposed_fix: Report, for the lab x loss-framing cell specifically (and ideally for each cell in Table 5): the number of underlying estimates and studies, the implied minimum detectable effect size at conventional power (e.g., 80%) given that cell's precision, and a sensitivity check showing how the 0.07 estimate and its CI move when the studies contributing to that cell are perturbed (e.g., add/drop the largest-N study in the cell).
risk_of_fix: If the cell turns out to be very small (a handful of studies), reporting its size transparently could itself become the paper's most damaging admission -- the authors might be tempted to soften the headline language preemptively rather than simply disclosing the number, which would be the wrong response (disclosure, not reframing, is the fix).

logical-validity.reason: Quote: 'The Lombard effect: i) no correlation...and ii) linear function.' Motivation clearly stated.

quote: Three of the co-authors collected 1/3 of the data each; another co-author randomly checked 1/3 of the entire dataset. The discovered inconsistencies in coding were discussed among the co-authors and corrected for the entire dataset.
issue: This is the paper's only account of how the 48-variable, >100,000-data-point hand-coding exercise was quality-controlled. It describes a spot-check by a single co-author over one third of the data and an informal 'discussed among the co-authors' resolution process, but reports no inter-coder reliability statistic (e.g., Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa, percent agreement, or even a count of how many discrepancies were found and in which variables). For a meta-analysis whose entire heterogeneity/BMA apparatus depends on these 48 hand-coded moderators being measured consistently, the absence of any quantitative reliability check on the coding itself -- only a description of an informal cross-check -- is a missing validation step a rigorous reader would expect (analogous to reporting inter-rater reliability in any systematic-review/PRISMA-style protocol).
why_it_matters: If the 35 usable moderators that feed into BMA are noisily or inconsistently coded, the entire heterogeneity analysis (and the headline lab/loss-framing moderator finding built on it) inherits that measurement error -- attenuating some coefficients, inflating others, and making posterior-inclusion-probability rankings less trustworthy than they appear. A one-sentence description of an ad hoc spot-check, with no number attached, leaves this risk completely unquantified for what is otherwise a heavily statistics-forward paper.
proposed_fix: Report a quantitative inter-coder reliability measure (e.g., percent agreement or kappa) for the cross-checked third of the dataset, broken down by variable or variable group, and disclose how many discrepancies were found per 48 variables before the 'discussed and corrected' resolution.
risk_of_fix: Computing reliability statistics retroactively from the original coding sheets (before correction) may not be feasible if the discrepancies were corrected in place rather than logged; the authors may only be able to report a post hoc reconstruction, which itself would need a caveat about its limits.

location.section: 1 Introduction / 2 Data and Experimental Context (search-strategy description and Figure A1-A3 PRISMA diagrams)

issue: PRISMA flow diagrams are used to document the search-and-screening funnel (Figures A1-A3), but the paper never states that the meta-analysis protocol itself -- the inclusion criteria, the moderator list, the choice of PCC as the common-currency metric, the winsorizing threshold, the planned bias-correction battery, or the BMA specification -- was registered ex ante (e.g., in PROSPERO, OSF, or as a pre-analysis plan) before the data were collected and inspected. PRISMA documents what was searched and found; it says nothing about whether the analytic choices were locked down beforehand or adapted after seeing the data. Given the very large garden-of-forking-paths the central tensions flag (>30 billion BMA models, a battery of 6+ bias-correction techniques, a 'preferred vs non-preferred' classification that is itself a judgment call), the absence of any statement about ex ante registration of the analysis plan -- as opposed to merely the search protocol -- is a load-bearing gap.
why_it_matters: Without a registered ex ante analysis plan, a skeptical reader cannot rule out that some of the consequential choices that shape the headline (which correction technique to designate 'preferred', which 35-of-48 moderators to retain, the winsorizing threshold, the definition of 'best practice' used to compute the 0.03 implied effect) were made, even partly, with knowledge of how they would affect the bottom-line numbers. This is exactly the kind of silent gap that converts an otherwise-rigorous meta-analysis into one whose robustness checks cannot fully discipline a motivated search through specifications -- a concern the paper's own central tensions explicitly flag as live.
proposed_fix: State explicitly whether (and where) an ex ante analysis plan was registered before data collection/inspection began, and if none was registered, add a transparency statement acknowledging that the analytic choices (preferred-correction designation, moderator retention, winsorizing threshold, 'best practice' definition) were made after seeing preliminary results, with a discussion of how that affects the interpretation of the robustness battery.
risk_of_fix: If no pre-registration exists (likely, since none is mentioned), simply adding the disclosure could read as an admission that invites further scrutiny of every downstream choice; the authors may prefer to argue (defensibly) that meta-analyses of already-published literatures are not well-suited to pre-registration in the same way primary experiments are -- but that argument itself needs to be made explicitly rather than left silent.

logical-validity.reason: Quote: '0.07, with a 95% confidence interval of (0.01, 0.14).' Direct match from text.

quote: These experiments also tend to have low power. Esteves-Sorenson & Broce (2022) report that across the 82 papers they review, the median number of subjects per experimental condition was merely 15.
issue: The paper acknowledges -- via a citation to a different study -- that the underlying experimental literature is plausibly underpowered, and even floats this as a candidate explanation for the null headline result later ('economics experiments have, on average, failed to detect the underlying positive effects of incentives due to measurement error and limited statistical power'). Yet the paper never performs its own power/precision diagnostic on its actual collected sample of 2,193 estimates / 88 studies (e.g., a retrospective power curve, a funnel-based assessment of how many included estimates could even in principle have detected a 'small' Doucouliagos-scale PCC of 0.07-0.17 at conventional power). It borrows someone else's power claim as a post hoc explanatory hand-wave rather than quantifying power within its own dataset -- a striking omission for a paper that otherwise builds an elaborate statistical apparatus.
why_it_matters: If the included literature is, on the authors' own telling, systematically underpowered, that fact bears directly on how to interpret a 'close to zero and statistically insignificant' corrected mean: a null result from underpowered primary studies is not the same evidential object as a null result from well-powered ones, and the corrected-mean machinery (linear/nonlinear bias correction, MAIVE, BMA) does not by itself fix a power problem in the underlying estimates. Without the paper's own power analysis, the reader cannot tell whether 'close to zero' means 'the true effect is close to zero' or 'the literature could not have detected anything but close-to-zero regardless of the true effect' -- two very different conclusions that license very different policy claims.
proposed_fix: Add a retrospective power/precision analysis of the collected sample -- e.g., compute the proportion of included estimates that would have had at least 80% power to detect a PCC of 0.07 (the paper's own headline 'exception' magnitude) or 0.17 ('small' per Doucouliagos), and discuss how that proportion qualifies the interpretation of the near-zero corrected mean.
risk_of_fix: A retrospective power calculation requires assumptions about the 'true' effect size being tested for, which is somewhat circular in a meta-analysis whose entire purpose is to estimate that effect; the authors would need to be careful to frame the exercise as illustrative (power to detect specific benchmark magnitudes) rather than as an independent estimate of the truth.

logical-validity.reason: Quote: 'evidence on the experimental margin that economists have chosen.' Scope explicitly stated.

location.section: 3 Publication Bias (robustness paragraph, and Appendix Tables B6-B9)

issue: The robustness battery reported (non-winsorized data, expanded Cohen's-d dataset, working-paper subset, one-estimate-per-study/experiment, preferred-vs-non-preferred) never includes a leave-one-study-out (or leave-one-out by source/journal) analysis -- i.e., systematically dropping each of the 88 (or 54 baseline) studies in turn and checking whether the corrected mean effect, the publication-bias slope, or the lab+loss-framing exception survives. Given that the paper itself documents extreme concentration of estimates within studies (93% of studies contribute multiple estimates, averaging 25 per study), a single influential study could be disproportionately responsible for either the overall near-zero corrected mean or the one positive exception, and the reader has no way to assess that from the reported checks.
why_it_matters: Leave-one-out analysis is a standard, low-cost robustness check in meta-analysis precisely because heavily-clustered data (as this paper's own dependence-structure description implies) can be dominated by one or two outsized contributors. Its absence means the paper cannot rule out that either its headline null or its headline lab+loss-framing exception is substantially an artifact of one or two studies -- a vulnerability that goes to the heart of whether the central claims are 'discovery or curation' (a tension the brief itself flags).
proposed_fix: Add a leave-one-study-out (and/or leave-one-journal-out) robustness exercise reporting the range of the corrected mean effect and the lab+loss-framing implied estimate across all iterations, ideally visualized (e.g., a forest-style plot of the corrected mean as each study is excluded).
risk_of_fix: With 88 (or 54) studies and an already-elaborate battery of corrections, adding 88 reruns of the full pipeline (bias correction + BMA) could be computationally heavy; the authors may need to scope the exercise to the linear/MAIVE corrected mean and the lab+loss-framing cell rather than the entire BMA exercise, and should say so explicitly to avoid implying broader coverage than delivered.

location.section: 3 Publication Bias / Table 2 and Table 5 (reporting of corrected means and implied estimates)

issue: Throughout the corrected-mean and implied-estimate reporting (the 0.03 'best practice' figure, the 0.025 Lazear/Angrist-Lavy figure, and the per-context implied estimates in Table 5 other than the singled-out 0.07 lab+loss cell), the paper reports point estimates and significance levels but never a prediction interval -- the range within which a new study's true effect would be expected to fall, given the estimated heterogeneity (tau^2) across the 88 studies. A confidence interval describes uncertainty about the mean; a prediction interval describes the dispersion of true study-level effects, which is what a practitioner deciding whether to use incentives in their own context actually needs. The paper documents substantial heterogeneity informally ('there is also substantial heterogeneity' from the funnel plot, Figure 1's 'median estimates... typically range between 0 and 0.2... some studies report values as low as -0.2 or as high as 0.4') but never translates that into a formal prediction interval around any of its headline corrected-mean numbers.
why_it_matters: The paper's policy-relevant framing ('increasing financial rewards rarely produces large performance gains') is a claim about what a manager or policymaker should expect in their own setting -- which is precisely the question a prediction interval answers and a confidence interval does not. Given the paper's own evidence of wide study-level dispersion (effects ranging from -0.2 to 0.4), a prediction interval around the 0.03 corrected mean could plausibly span both 'negligible' and 'small-to-moderate' by the paper's own Doucouliagos benchmarks, materially complicating the 'rarely produces large gains' framing that the abstract and conclusion foreground.
proposed_fix: Report a prediction interval (using the estimated between-study heterogeneity variance, e.g., tau^2 from a random-effects specification) alongside the headline corrected-mean estimates in Table 2 and/or Table 5, and discuss explicitly what that interval implies for an individual practitioner's expected experience versus the population-average claim the abstract makes.
risk_of_fix: Computing a credible prediction interval requires a properly estimated between-study heterogeneity variance from a random-effects (not fixed-effects/clustered-OLS) specification; bolting one onto the existing clustered-OLS / MAIVE framework without care could produce an interval whose assumptions are inconsistent with the rest of the paper's estimation choices, creating a new internal-consistency problem.

quote: Markov chain Monte Carlo algorithm (Zeugner & Feldkircher, 2015) to walk only through the most important part of the model mass
issue: The paper states that, because the BMA model space exceeds 30 billion candidate models, an MCMC algorithm is used to sample it -- but it never reports any convergence diagnostics for that sampler (e.g., chain length / number of draws, burn-in, the correlation between analytical and MCMC-based posterior model probabilities that the BMS package conventionally reports, or any check that the walk actually covered the high-probability region rather than getting stuck in a local mode). For an exercise whose entire credibility rests on the MCMC having adequately explored a combinatorial space this large, the absence of any stated convergence check is a load-bearing methodological gap that a careful referee in the Bayesian-econometrics tradition would flag immediately.
why_it_matters: If the MCMC walk did not converge or only sampled a non-representative slice of the 30-billion-model space, the reported posterior inclusion probabilities (PIP=1 for standard error, the framing and lab coefficients that anchor the headline heterogeneity story) could be artifacts of where the chain happened to wander rather than stable features of the posterior. Because the paper's single positive finding (lab + loss framing) is identified through this BMA exercise, an unreported or failed convergence check would undermine the very mechanism by which that finding is supposed to be 'robust.'
proposed_fix: Report standard MCMC convergence diagnostics for the BMA exercise -- e.g., the number of MCMC draws/burn-in used, the correlation between MCMC iteration counts and analytical (exact) posterior model probabilities for the top models (a diagnostic the BMS package computes natively), and/or a sensitivity check re-running the chain with a different random seed or longer walk to confirm stability of the PIP rankings.
risk_of_fix: If convergence diagnostics reveal instability, the authors would face a more serious problem than a presentational gap -- so this fix carries the risk of surfacing a finding that requires re-running (and possibly revising) the entire heterogeneity section; that is a genuine possible outcome of doing the check honestly, not a flaw in the check itself.

location.section: 1 Introduction / 5 Conclusion (discussion of the lab + loss-framing exception and its proposed explanations)

issue: The paper offers two competing explanations for why the corrected effect is positive specifically in the lab+loss-framing cell and near-zero elsewhere -- the 'distraction effect' (citing Rusz et al. 2020, more pronounced in field settings) and a measurement-error/low-power story (citing Esteves-Sorenson & Broce 2022) -- but never designs or reports any analysis that would discriminate between them, nor any falsification/placebo check that would stress-test either story (e.g., does the lab effect appear, or fail to appear, in a placebo cell where the distraction-effect mechanism predicts it should not; does the framing effect persist when restricted to high-powered studies only, which would favor the distraction story over the low-power story). Both explanations are floated as 'possible' and left untested side by side.
why_it_matters: Offering two mutually exclusive causal stories for the paper's single positive finding without any test that could favor one over the other leaves the central interpretive payoff of the heterogeneity section essentially unfalsifiable as stated -- a reader cannot tell whether the 'distraction effect' framing that the abstract and conclusion lean on for color is anything more than a plausible-sounding label attached after the fact to a borderline statistical cell. A meta-analysis that goes to the trouble of building an elaborate moderator-coding and BMA apparatus could, in principle, design a test that discriminates between a measurement/power story (which would predict the lab effect strengthens when restricting to higher-powered subsamples) and a distraction story (which would predict the effect tracks proxies for reward salience/cue-visibility rather than study power) -- but no such test is attempted.
proposed_fix: Add a discriminating test between the two candidate explanations -- e.g., interact the lab/framing moderators with a study-power proxy (sample size, degrees of freedom) and check whether the lab-effect strengthens or weakens in higher-powered subsamples (favoring the power story if it strengthens, the distraction story if it persists regardless of power), or construct a placebo cell where the distraction mechanism would not predict an effect and check that none appears there.
risk_of_fix: Constructing a clean discriminating test post hoc risks becoming just one more specification in the garden of forking paths the central tensions already worry about; the authors would need to pre-commit to the test's design and interpretation before running it (or run it on a held-out subsample) to avoid simply adding another contestable robustness cell to an already-crowded battery.

quote: The Bayesian approach, however, treats all observations as independent, and to account for within-study dependence we also employ frequentist model averaging with Mallow's weights (Hansen, 2007) and orthogonalization of model space according to Amini & Parmeter (2012).
issue: Within-study dependence handling in BMA heterogeneity analysis is partially addressed: the paper acknowledges BMA treats observations as independent and employs frequentist model averaging (FMA) with Mallows weights as a robustness check. However, the main reported results (Table 4) feature BMA estimates without explicit study-level clustering; only the FMA supplement addresses within-study correlation. The paper does not compare BMA and FMA coefficients directly or discuss whether they diverge materially, which would demonstrate whether ignoring within-study dependence in BMA meaningfully biases the heterogeneity findings.
why_it_matters: Table 4 (BMA results) is a primary evidence source for which moderators robustly predict heterogeneity (e.g., lab setting, loss framing). If within-study dependence inflates the apparent precision of BMA posteriors, claims about posterior-inclusion probabilities (PIP) and coefficient significance could overstate robustness. The paper does not show that the BMA and FMA moderator findings converge, leaving ambiguity about whether the headline heterogeneity claims (lab+loss frame effect) rest on assumptions violated in the BMA leg of the analysis.
proposed_fix: Report Table 4 results in a side-by-side comparison with the FMA equivalent, showing posterior means, SDs, and PIPs for both BMA and FMA for all variables. If the two approaches differ materially for key moderators (lab, loss framing, standard error), flag the difference and discuss implications. If they agree, report that explicitly to affirm robustness.
risk_of_fix: None; this is a transparency addition. If FMA and BMA diverge substantially on key moderators, the authors would need to investigate whether heterogeneity claims hold under the more defensible (study-clustered) approach.

issue: The paper claims 'different weights do not change the conclusion, and any systematic differences seem to be small' (p. 12) but the actual numerical comparison of weighted versus unweighted means is not shown in Table 1 or nearby. The table footnote defines the weighting approaches but does not display side-by-side point estimates and confidence intervals for unweighted vs. weighted-by-inverse-number-per-study vs. precision-weighted results. Readers cannot verify the magnitude of 'small' differences or assess whether any weighting scheme moves the mean effect meaningfully.
why_it_matters: The paper's defense of the PCC metric rests partly on showing insensitivity to weighting; absence of numerical comparison weakens this empirical claim. The largest effect the paper reports is 0.07 (lab+loss frame, on the threshold between negligible and small per Doucouliagos 2011). If different weighting schemes yield notably different implied means, the apparent consensus would be less robust.
proposed_fix: In Table 1 or an appendix table, add columns reporting the mean PCC under at least three weighting schemes (unweighted, inverse-number-per-study, precision-weighted) with confidence intervals for baseline, expanded, and working-paper samples. This would allow readers to assess the actual magnitude of differences across weighting approaches.
risk_of_fix: None; this is presentation. If the ranges are non-negligible, the authors should discuss.

quote: For 93% of the studies we collect multiple estimates, with an average of 25 estimates included per study.
issue: Study-level clustering of standard errors is employed across all main analyses to account for within-study dependence. However, with 93% of studies contributing an average of 25 estimates, and many derived from overlapping subsamples, treatment arms, and model specifications within the same study, clustering at the study level may be insufficient. The paper does not report intra-cluster correlation coefficients or test sensitivity to finer clustering levels. Table B8 in the appendix shows experiment-level clustering is possible, but main results rely on study-level clustering throughout without visible justification for this choice.
why_it_matters: If within-study estimates are correlated at ICC > 0.05 (common in hierarchical data), study-level clustering may underestimate standard errors and inflate false-positive rates for moderator effects. The headline heterogeneity findings (lab+loss frame effect = 0.07, key moderators in Table 4) depend on the precision of coefficient estimates; if SEs are systematically underestimated, confidence intervals are too narrow.
proposed_fix: Estimate intra-cluster correlations for within-study estimates by outcome type. Re-estimate main results (Table 2 key coefficients, Table 4 heterogeneity) using experiment-level clustering and confirm coefficient SEs and significance do not change materially. Report in an appendix robustness table.
risk_of_fix: If experiment-level clustering yields substantially larger SEs (>20% increase), some moderator effects in Table 4 may drop below PIP = 0.5 or significance thresholds. This is not a flaw but a finding to surface.

quote:
The Bayesian approach, however,
treats all observations as independent, and to account for within-study dependence we also
employ frequentist model averaging with Mallow's weights (Hansen, 2007) and orthogonalization
issue: The paper's central headline moderator finding -- the 'lab + loss framing' exception (PCC ~0.07, the only positive result in the paper) -- is identified primarily through the Bayesian model-averaging exercise (Table 4, Figure 6, PIP=1 for SE/framing/lab). The authors themselves admit this Bayesian engine 'treats all observations as independent,' i.e. it ignores that 93% of the 2,193 estimates are nested in just 88 studies (avg. 25/study, many sharing subject pools, specifications, and treatment arms). The only attempt to handle this dependence -- frequentist model averaging with Mallow's weights -- is explicitly demoted to a 'robustness check,' meaning the paper's preferred, headline-generating procedure is the one that gets the dependence structure wrong, while the dependence-aware procedure is relegated to secondary status. This inverts the natural priority: the analysis that respects the actual data-generating/sampling structure should be the baseline, not the check.
proposed_fix: Make the dependence-aware frequentist model-averaging exercise (with Mallow's weights and orthogonalization) the primary/baseline heterogeneity analysis, or at minimum report both baseline and robustness results side-by-side with equal prominence in the main text (not just the Appendix), and explicitly discuss whether the headline lab+loss-framing result (PIP, posterior mean, CI) is materially different once within-study dependence is modeled rather than assumed away.
risk_of_fix: Re-running BMA with a dependence-respecting framework could change which moderators cross the PIP=0.5 threshold or shift point estimates enough that the lab+loss-framing 'exception' loses significance or magnitude -- which would remove the paper's only positive finding and require reframing the abstract/conclusion. That is a real risk to the paper's contribution, not an artifact of the fix; if it materializes, it indicates the original headline was an artifact of the independence assumption rather than the fix being wrong.

logical-validity.reason: Table 2 constants near zero across methods (0.002-0.0675 range). Inference logically sound.

location.section: Appendix B (Multiple estimates per study) / Section 3 Table 2 notes

quote: For 93% of the studies we collect multiple estimates, with an average of 25 estimates included per study
issue: Single-level clustering at the study level is the paper's sole adjustment for dependence in every linear/meta-regression specification (Table 2, Table B8, etc.), yet the paper's own description of why studies yield ~25 estimates each reveals at least three distinct, nested sources of correlation that a flat one-way study cluster cannot distinguish: (i) multiple specifications run on the *same* sample/regression (mechanically correlated coefficients and standard errors), (ii) multiple treatment arms within one experiment (estimates sharing a common control group), and (iii) multiple experiments within one study (a coarser grouping than 'experiment' but finer than 'study'). Treating all ~25 estimates per study as exchangeable members of one cluster, when some pairs share an entire regression sample and others merely share an author team, materially understates the true effective sample size used for inference (the cluster-robust variance estimator's asymptotics assume a moderate number of roughly homogeneous, independent clusters -- 88 clusters of wildly heterogeneous internal correlation structure is a known stress case).
proposed_fix: Report a multi-way or nested clustering scheme (e.g., cluster by study AND by experiment/specification-family, or a wild-cluster bootstrap with the small, heterogeneous number of 88 clusters) as the primary inference approach, and show how the headline publication-bias and corrected-mean estimates (Table 2) and the heterogeneity results (Table 4) move under that scheme versus the current flat study-level clustering.
risk_of_fix: With only 88 clusters that vary enormously in internal estimate count (1 to >100) and structure, more granular clustering could inflate standard errors so much that even the 'robust' findings (publication bias itself, the corrected mean near zero) lose statistical significance -- which would be informative but could be read as 'breaking' a result that the authors consider solid. The fix could also be technically difficult to execute cleanly given how heterogeneous the within-study estimate structure is (the paper itself says it varies study by study).

logical-validity.reason: Table 2 Panel A: OLS slope 0.854 (0.255). Direct match; statistically significant.

location.section: 2 Data and Experimental Context (PCC formula, eq. 1)

quote: where t stands for the t-statistic of the reported coefficient and df indicates the number of degrees of freedom in the estimation
issue: The PCC formula (t / sqrt(t^2 + df)) is presented as THE mechanism that converts incommensurable outcome measures (grades, game scores, charitable donations, work output, time-to-completion) into a single comparable metric. But the formula's comparability hinges entirely on 't' and 'df' meaning the same statistical thing across the 88 primary studies. The paper never discusses whether the 'degrees of freedom' it collects are computed consistently across studies that use very different inference frameworks -- e.g., a study with cluster-robust standard errors at the subject level reports an effective df that is not the residual df of an OLS regression on the full sample; fixed-effects panel models, multi-level/hierarchical models, and bootstrap-based inference each define 'df' differently or not at all in the classical sense. If primary studies' reported df values are not on a common footing, the resulting PCCs -- despite their superficial numerical comparability -- are not actually standardized onto a common scale, undermining the paper's central claim that PCC is a valid 'common currency' (the very property the formula is invoked to deliver).
proposed_fix: Add a methodological discussion (in Section 2 alongside eq. 1, not buried in an appendix) of how 'degrees of freedom' was operationalized across the heterogeneous estimation frameworks in the 88 primary studies (OLS, FE, logit/probit/tobit, DID, clustered/robust SE, bootstrap), whether any adjustment was made when a study's reported inference framework makes 'df' ambiguous or non-classical, and ideally a sensitivity check restricting to the subset of studies using directly comparable (e.g., simple OLS with reported residual df) specifications.
risk_of_fix: If the authors discover that df comparability genuinely varies across the sample, any correction (e.g., dropping non-comparable estimates, or imputing an alternative df) would change the PCC values feeding every downstream table -- a substantial re-run that could alter headline numbers. A poorly-specified correction could also introduce new, harder-to-detect comparability problems (e.g., privileging studies whose df happens to be easiest to standardize).

logical-validity.reason: Specific p-values from tables. Cannot confirm exact numbers from text extraction.

location.section: Table 3 (Description and summary statistics of regression variables -- 'Effect: negative')

quote: = 1 if the proxy for performance i
issue: The procedure for harmonizing the *sign* of the PCC across outcome measures with opposite polarity (e.g., 'time to finish a task,' where a negative coefficient on the incentive means BETTER performance, versus 'quantity produced,' where positive means better) is disclosed only as a one-line aside inside a Table-3 variable definition ('...has to be multiplied by -1 for consistency in our meta-analysis'), not in Section 2 where the PCC formula and aggregation are introduced and where a reader would need it to assess whether pooling 2,193 estimates into one mean PCC is even coherent. Worse, this hand-applied sign-flip is itself a discretionary coding decision made by the same co-author team that 'filled more than 100,000 data points by hand' (a process the paper says was checked by re-coding only 1/3 of the dataset) -- yet 'Effect: positive' subsequently appears as a moderator in the BMA/heterogeneity analysis (Table 4: posterior mean 0.013, PIP 0.461) with a non-trivial estimated relationship to the (supposedly already-harmonized) PCC. If the harmonization fully removed the sign artifact, 'Effect: positive' should carry no residual explanatory power over the response variable it was used to construct/clean; its surviving PIP suggests either incomplete harmonization, a confound between measurement-direction and substantive context (e.g., lab tasks disproportionately use 'positive' proxies), or both -- any of which casts doubt on whether the pooled PCC numbers reported as the headline (0.051, 0.03, 0.07) are measuring a single coherent construct.
proposed_fix: Move the sign-harmonization rule into Section 2 as an explicit, prominent step in the PCC construction pipeline (before eq. 1's output is used in any pooling), report how many of the 2,193 estimates were sign-flipped, and explain -- or test directly -- why 'Effect: positive/negative' retains explanatory power in BMA after the harmonization is supposedly already baked into the response variable (e.g., is it proxying for task type rather than measurement artifact?).
risk_of_fix: Investigating this could reveal that some estimates were mis-flipped or inconsistently coded, requiring a correction to the underlying PCC values used throughout -- a substantial re-derivation. Conversely, if the authors show 'Effect: positive' is capturing a genuine substantive pattern (not a harmonization artifact), the fix is just an expository move with low risk; the risk is concentrated in the scenario where the investigation surfaces a real coding error.

logical-validity.reason: Quote: 'employ Bayesian model averaging...natural solution to model uncertainty.' Method and rationale stated.

location.section: 2 Data and Experimental Context / 3 Publication Bias (Section introducing PCC and clustering)

issue: Nowhere does the paper discuss -- or test -- whether the partial correlation coefficient itself is comparable across the very different statistical models from which it is extracted. A PCC computed from a simple bivariate OLS t-statistic and an PCC computed from a t-statistic on a single coefficient inside a saturated fixed-effects panel regression with dozens of controls are not measuring 'the same thing' in any straightforward sense -- the latter's t-statistic (and hence PCC) is partialling out a completely different (and study-specific) set of confounders, so the 'partial' in 'partial correlation' means something different study to study. The paper presents PCC as if it neutralizes model heterogeneity ('the point estimates cannot be compared directly. We thus recompute them to partial correlation coefficients...for comparability'), but converting to a partial correlation does not equalize what is being partialled out. This is a foundational, load-bearing assumption of the entire meta-analysis -- it determines whether 2,193 numbers can be meaningfully averaged at all -- and it receives no acknowledgment, test, or even a caveat anywhere in the manuscript or appendix.
proposed_fix: Add an explicit discussion (with citation to the methodological literature on PCC comparability across differently-specified primary models, e.g., Stanley & Doucouliagos 2012 and the critiques in Stanley et al. 2024/2025 already cited elsewhere in the paper) acknowledging that PCCs from differently-saturated models partial out different confounder sets, and report a robustness check restricted to primary-study specifications with comparable degrees of model saturation (e.g., 'parsimonious' vs. 'fully controlled' subsets).
risk_of_fix: A frank discussion of this limitation could (correctly) weaken the paper's central comparability claim and invite reviewers to ask for a robustness sample that may be too small to support the meta-analysis at all -- a structural risk inherent to the honest answer, not to a badly-designed fix.

logical-validity.reason: Benabou & Tirole (2003, 2011) and Sliwka (2007) models discussed. Intrinsic motivation theory integrated.

location.section: 3 Publication Bias (robustness paragraph referencing Table B8)

quote: Our results do not change substantially if we consider just one estimate per study or one estimate per experiment.
issue: This is offered as the paper's main reassurance that within-study/within-experiment dependence does not drive the results, but it only checks the *publication-bias correction* (Table B8 reports the same OLS/W-Study/BE-Study/W-Experiment/BE-Experiment panel structure as Table 2). It is never extended to the heterogeneity/BMA exercise -- the very place where the paper's headline positive finding (lab + loss framing, PCC ~0.07, 'on the threshold between negligible and small') lives, and where, per F1 above, dependence is explicitly assumed away. A reassurance that the *mean* is robust to one-estimate-per-study subsetting says nothing about whether a *moderator* result built on 2,193 correlated observations and a 35-variable BMA search would survive the same collapse to ~88-200 independent observations -- a search with a much higher ratio of candidate explanations to truly independent data points than the headline-mean exercise.
proposed_fix: Re-run the BMA/heterogeneity analysis (or at minimum the lab+loss-framing specification) on the one-estimate-per-study and one-estimate-per-experiment subsets used in Table B8, and report whether the PIPs and posterior means for 'Laboratory experiment' and 'Negative framing' survive at comparable magnitude and precision with an order-of-magnitude fewer (and truly independent) observations.
risk_of_fix: With only ~88-200 independent observations, a 35-variable BMA is likely to be severely underpowered -- the check could legitimately fail to replicate the lab+loss-framing result not because the original is wrong but because the subsetted analysis has too little power to detect anything. The authors would then need to communicate that nuance carefully to avoid the check being read as a refutation when it may simply be underpowered.

location.section: 3 Publication Bias (Table 2 weighting columns / Section 2 weighting discussion)

issue: The paper offers two weighting regimes throughout (unweighted = each estimate counted equally; 'Study'/'Weighted' = inverse of the number of estimates per study, giving each study equal weight) but never weights by precision *and* study membership jointly, nor does it discuss -- or even flag as an open question -- which weighting scheme is theoretically appropriate given that the within-study estimate count (1 to 107+, per Figure 3's N values) is itself plausibly correlated with study quality, sample size, or the very publication-bias mechanisms the paper is trying to correct (a study that ran more specifications/treatment arms to find a publishable result would, under 'each study counts equally,' have its 25 fishing-expedition estimates collapsed to the same weight as another study's 1 clean estimate -- diluting exactly the signal the publication-bias correction is designed to detect). This is a load-bearing methodological choice with no stated justification beyond 'different weights do not change the conclusion.'
proposed_fix: Add a brief discussion of the theoretical tradeoffs between equal-estimate, equal-study, and precision weighting in the presence of the specific dependence structure described in Appendix B (multiple specifications/treatment arms/subsamples), and report whether the number of estimates per study correlates with study-level characteristics (sample size, publication venue tier, year) that are themselves related to the publication-bias mechanism -- which would make the 'equal study weight' choice not neutral but a substantive modeling decision.
risk_of_fix: Exploring this could reveal that the choice of weighting scheme is not in fact innocuous (contrary to the current 'differences seem to be small' claim), forcing a re-derivation of headline numbers under the theoretically-preferred scheme -- a substantial and potentially headline-moving piece of work that the authors may reasonably resist taking on for a meta-analytic choice that is conventional in the field.

quote: which yield a mean partial correlation of 0.07, with a 95% confidence interval of (0.01, 0.14)
issue: The paper's single positive headline finding -- the joint 'laboratory + loss (negative) framing' implied effect of about 0.07 -- is stated repeatedly in prose (Abstract, Introduction, Heterogeneity section, Conclusion) but never appears as a tabulated cell anywhere the reader can check it. Table 5 ('Effects implied for different contexts'), which is explicitly billed as 'the bottom line of our analysis' and the source of implied-context PCCs, reports each moderator's implied effect one at a time (e.g., 'Laboratory experiment 0.073', 'Negative framing 0.066') but never the joint lab-times-loss-framing cell. A careful reader who wants to verify or locate the provenance of the 0.07 number that anchors the abstract has to either re-derive an interaction from marginal effects (which is not how BMA fitted values combine, and 0.073 and 0.066 do not obviously average or compound to 0.07) or take the number entirely on faith. This is exactly the kind of 'reconstruct the headline number from the tables without re-deriving it' gap the paper's presentation should close, and it concerns the more newsworthy of the paper's two headline numbers (the positive exception, not the near-zero baseline).
proposed_fix: Add an explicit row (or a clearly labeled sub-panel) to Table 5 -- or a companion table/figure -- reporting the implied PCC (and CI) for the joint laboratory-experiment x negative-framing cell, with a one-line note on how it was computed (e.g., fitted value setting both dummies to 1, all else at the stated reference values). Cross-reference that exact cell from the Abstract/Introduction sentence that states the 0.07 figure.
risk_of_fix: If the joint cell was obtained via a different specification or sub-sample than the rest of Table 5 (e.g., a separate interaction-term regression rather than a fitted-value combination of the two main-effect coefficients), simply inserting it without documenting that difference could create a new internal-consistency question; the authors should be explicit about exactly which model produced the 0.07 figure.

location.section: Section 4 Heterogeneity, final paragraph before Conclusion (p.30)

quote: The overall mean incentive-performance effect based on our definition of "best practice" described above is 0.03.
issue: The prose rounds the 'best practice' headline figure to 0.03 ('is 0.03'), while the corresponding row of Table 5 reports it to three decimals as 0.031. Because this is the number the Abstract and the seat's own justifying material foreground as the paper's central corrected estimate, the rounding mismatch between the in-text statement and its tabulated source (0.03 vs 0.031) is a small but avoidable inconsistency that a careful referee or reader cross-checking the number will notice -- especially given that the paper otherwise reports most quantities to two or three decimals (e.g., 0.051, 0.069, 0.07).
proposed_fix: Either state the figure to the same precision as Table 5 ('is 0.031') or, if 0.03 is the intended rounded headline figure for readability, add a parenthetical pointing to the precise tabulated value, e.g., 'is 0.03 (0.031 in Table 5)'.
risk_of_fix: Minimal; this is a cosmetic rounding alignment and changes no substantive claim.

location.table_or_figure: cf. Section 2: 'Fifty-four studies satisfy our inclusion criteria...' and 'In total, in this meta-analysis we consider 88 studies'

quote: has been noted by only 27 of the 54 economics studies we collect for our baseline analysis
issue: The manuscript uses two different headline counts of 'studies' -- 54 and 88 -- in ways that are internally consistent once parsed carefully (54 = peer-reviewed baseline studies that define 'primary studies'; 88 = 54 + 19 working papers + additional snowballed studies in the expanded/Cohen's-d dataset) but are not signposted at the point of use. The sentence at issue refers to 'the 54 economics studies we collect for our baseline analysis' immediately after the paper has spent a full page emphasizing '88 economics experiments' (Abstract) and 'we consider 88 studies' (Section 2, end). A reader who has just absorbed '88' as the headline sample size encounters '54' described as 'our baseline analysis' sample without an explicit reminder of how the two relate, inviting a moment of confusion about which number is the 'real' baseline N.
proposed_fix: At first use of '54' in Section 3 (or by adding a short parenthetical), remind the reader of the relationship, e.g., '...noted by only 27 of the 54 peer-reviewed studies that make up our baseline sample (out of 88 studies in total once working papers and snowballed studies are included)'.
risk_of_fix: Very low; purely additive clarification, does not touch any number or claim.

quote: using orthogonalization of covariate space suggested Amini & Parmeter (2012) to reduce the number of estimated models
issue: A grammatical slip in the Table 4 notes -- 'orthogonalization of covariate space suggested Amini & Parmeter (2012)' is missing the preposition 'by' (it should read '...suggested by Amini & Parmeter (2012)'). This is a minor copy-editing lapse, but it sits in the notes of one of the paper's two central results tables (the BMA/FMA table the seat is specifically charged with checking for self-containedness), and similar phrasing elsewhere in the body text ('orthogonalization of model space according to Amini & Parmeter (2012)', Introduction) shows the authors know the correct construction, making this a one-off slip rather than a stylistic choice.
proposed_fix: Insert 'by': '...using orthogonalization of covariate space suggested by Amini & Parmeter (2012) to reduce the number of estimated models...'.
risk_of_fix: None; pure copy-edit, no substantive content affected.

issue: Tables 4 and 5 -- the paper's central heterogeneity results, and the tables this seat was specifically asked to check for self-containedness -- never restate, in their own notes, the scale on which the reported partial correlation coefficients should be read (negligible/small/large per Doucouliagos 2011 thresholds of roughly <0.07, <0.17, >0.33). That interpretive scale is introduced once, in a footnote to Section 2 (footnote 4, attached to Figure 2's discussion), and the reader is expected to carry it, unstated, through ten more pages to correctly judge whether a Table 5 implied effect of 0.07 or 0.073 is 'negligible,' 'small,' or 'borderline.' For a results table that is explicitly billed as 'the bottom line of our analysis' and whose whole rhetorical point rests on classifying numbers as negligible vs. small vs. borderline, omitting even a one-line reminder of the classification thresholds in the table notes themselves makes the table less self-contained than it could be -- a reader who encounters Table 5 without having Figure 2's footnote fresh in mind cannot, from the table alone, tell whether 0.073 or 0.066 should be read as meaningful or negligible.
proposed_fix: Add a one-sentence reminder to the notes of Table 4 and/or Table 5 restating the Doucouliagos (2011) negligible/small/large thresholds (or simply cross-reference footnote 4 explicitly: 'See footnote 4 for the negligible/small/large classification thresholds used to interpret these PCCs').
risk_of_fix: Essentially none; purely additive labeling that helps the reader without altering any number, claim, or analysis.

quote: we employ a battery of recently developed nonlinear tests (Ioannidis et al., 2017; Andrews & Kasy, 2019; Bom & Rachinger, 2019; Furukawa, 2020), which all corroborate our previous findings regarding publication bias and the mean underlying effect.
issue: Read in its strongest form, the correction battery is not a single fragile estimator dressed up with cosmetic robustness checks but a genuine triangulation across techniques with materially different identifying assumptions: linear meta-regression (Lombard-effect/uncorrelation logic), five nonlinear corrections (WAAP, Top10, stem-based, Andrews-Kasy selection, endogenous kink) that relax linearity, an instrumental-variable approach (MAIVE) that relaxes the uncorrelation assumption, p-uniform* which relies on neither assumption, and caliper/p-curve tests (Gerber & Malhotra; Elliott et al.) that test for bias directly from the t-statistic/p-value distribution without using the standard error as a regressor at all. That so many methods resting on different (and in places mutually incompatible) assumptions converge on 'substantial publication bias, near-zero corrected effect' is precisely the kind of cross-validation the meta-analysis methodology literature recommends as the antidote to any single technique's fragility -- and is considerably more thorough than the typical economics meta-analysis, which often reports only a linear funnel-asymmetry test (the very gap the authors note 'none of the psychology meta-analyses correct for publication bias' at all).
proposed_fix: Add one explicit sentence in Section 3 (after the battery is introduced) stating outright that the techniques were chosen specifically because they rest on non-overlapping identifying assumptions, so that convergence across them constitutes triangulation rather than redundancy -- this would make the (already strong) defensive logic visible to referees who might otherwise read the long list as an unmotivated kitchen-sink.
risk_of_fix: Minimal -- a one-sentence addition that merely makes explicit a logic the paper already follows; the only risk is overclaiming that the assumptions are fully orthogonal when some (e.g., p-uniform* and the IV approach) still share components (inverse-variance weighting, reliance on standard errors).

location.paragraph: paragraph introducing MAIVE, citing Table B10

quote: test of the Andrews-Kasy model, shown in Table B10 in the Appendix, suggests that in our case estimates are indeed correlated with standard errors even in the absence of publication bias, we prefer the MAIVE approach (available also as a web app at easymeta.org). MAIVE suggests strong publication bias and negligible mean effect beyond the bias.
issue: The rival's framing -- that MAIVE is anointed 'preferred' on the strength of a single specification test -- understates how much independent justification the paper actually offers before that test is invoked. The text first lays out, in general terms, *three distinct theoretical sources of endogeneity* in the standard meta-regression (measurement error in the standard error itself, reverse causality via clustering choices, and unobserved method-driven heterogeneity), explains *why* the inverse-square-root-of-degrees-of-freedom instrument should be immune to exactly those three sources ('correlated with the standard error by definition... does not suffer from the three sources of endogeneity described above'), and only THEN reports the Table B10 test as a confirmatory diagnostic that the endogeneity concern is empirically live in this dataset (not merely theoretical). On a generous reading, Table B10 is not the sole basis for the preference -- it is the empirical trigger that converts a general econometric worry (which could apply to any meta-analysis) into a dataset-specific reason to trust the IV approach over the selection-model alternative whose own identifying assumption (constant publication probability conditional on significance band) the test shows is violated here.
proposed_fix: Restructure the paragraph so the logical sequence -- (1) three theoretical sources of endogeneity in the baseline approach, (2) why the proposed instrument is immune to all three by construction, (3) the Table B10 test as confirmatory evidence the concern is empirically live -- is made explicit with connective language ('We therefore expect this instrument to dominate on theoretical grounds; Table B10 confirms the concern is empirically present in our data'), so referees do not mistake the empirical test for the sole warrant.
risk_of_fix: Low -- purely expository; the only risk is that spelling out the logic invites closer scrutiny of whether the instrument really is immune to all three sources (a question the rival seat is positioned to press, e.g., on whether degrees of freedom can itself proxy for method choices).

quote: Such an instrument is correlated with the standard error by the definition of the latter and can be expected to be less related to method choices.
issue: Even granting the instrument the most charitable reading, the exclusion-restriction defense offered here is a plausibility claim ('can be expected to be less related'), not a demonstrated property. Sample size / degrees of freedom is itself a design choice correlated with the very 'method choices' (e.g., whether a study uses a large lab sample vs. a small natural-experiment sample, whether clustering reduces effective observations, whether the study design is a within-subject vs. between-subject comparison) that the paper itself lists as one of the three endogeneity sources the instrument is supposed to escape. This is the one place where the rival's 'is the instrument plausibly excludable' challenge has real traction, and a generous reading should concede that the paper's hedge ('can be expected to') is doing real work -- it is an assumption the authors flag as an assumption, not a proven fact, and the discipline-wide MAIVE literature (Irsova et al. 2025; Havranek et al. 2024) treats it the same way. The honest characterization is: the instrument is the best *currently available* solution to a genuinely hard identification problem, defended by analogy and by the corroborating Table B10 test rather than by a direct test of the exclusion restriction itself (which is, as in all IV settings, fundamentally untestable).
proposed_fix: Add an explicit sentence acknowledging that the exclusion restriction for the degrees-of-freedom instrument cannot be directly tested and is supported by plausibility argument and the corroborating Andrews-Kasy specification test rather than by a falsification test of the instrument itself -- and, ideally, report the over-identification or sensitivity analysis the MAIVE literature (Irsova et al. 2025) recommends for assessing how much the conclusion would change under a violated exclusion restriction.
risk_of_fix: Moderate -- naming the untestability explicitly could be read by a skeptical referee as conceding the rival's strongest point; but leaving it unsaid invites the same objection with less goodwill, so transparency is the lower-risk path. A poorly worded caveat could also overstate the doubt and undercut the 'preferred' designation the rest of the paper relies on.

quote: In addition, we use the tests of Gerber & Malhotra (2008) and Elliott et al. (2022), which also do not rely on the uncorrelation assumption and both corroborate publication bias.
issue: A skeptic could characterize the whole battery as 'currently fashionable techniques that all share the same blind spot.' The caliper test (Gerber & Malhotra 2008) and the Elliott et al. (2022) histogram-based p-curve tests are the strongest rebuttal to that charge: they operate directly on the distribution of t-statistics/p-values and explicitly do *not* use the standard error as a regressor or weighting variable at all, so they cannot share the endogeneity problem the paper itself identifies as afflicting the standard-error-based techniques. That these structurally different tests independently confirm publication bias (Table B1, Panel A: a jump in the t-statistic distribution at zero; Panel B: rejection of no-p-hacking for baseline/expanded/working-paper samples) is a genuinely independent line of evidence, not just another draw from the same well -- and the paper is commendably candid that the tests lose power on the smaller 'preferred-estimates' subsample rather than papering over that limitation.
proposed_fix: Promote the caliper/p-curve corroboration from an appendix afterthought to a sentence in the main-text Section 3 discussion of the battery, explicitly framing it as 'a test family that shares none of the standard-error-based assumptions of the rest of the battery, and which independently confirms the same conclusion' -- this directly forecloses the 'fashionable-techniques-with-shared-blind-spots' critique.
risk_of_fix: Very low -- moving an existing, already-reported result into more prominent framing; the only minor risk is lengthening an already dense methods section.

location.sentence: sentence reporting the p-uniform* corrected mean

quote: Once again we obtain evidence for publication bias, though the mean estimated incentive-performance effect is larger than in the previous cases.
issue: Granting the steelman that triangulation is the right strategy, the honest accounting must note that the techniques do not all converge on the same *number* -- only on the same *qualitative* verdict (substantial bias, small residual effect). p-uniform* yields a corrected mean (0.0675 per Table 2 Panel C) that is roughly twice MAIVE's (0.0181) and meaningfully closer to the 'small-effect' threshold the paper itself uses (Doucouliagos 2011 guidelines). A rigorous reader could ask whether 'negligible' is the right word for a range that spans roughly 0.018-0.07 depending on technique, and whether the paper's choice to foreground MAIVE's lower number (rather than, say, an average or range across the battery) as 'the' corrected effect is itself a form of selecting among methods. The paper is transparent that the estimates differ -- which is to its credit -- but the headline framing ('close to zero... negligible') compresses a real spread of point estimates into a single adjective.
proposed_fix: Add a sentence in Section 3 explicitly reporting the range of corrected-mean estimates across the full battery (not just MAIVE's), and briefly discuss why the preferred MAIVE estimate sits at the low end -- e.g., whether p-uniform*'s higher estimate reflects its own known limitations (loss of power from study-level aggregation, residual standard-error-based weighting) rather than a genuinely larger true effect. This converts an implicit number-shopping concern into an explicitly adjudicated one.
risk_of_fix: Low-to-moderate -- being explicit about the spread could be read as conceding more uncertainty than the headline currently implies, potentially softening the 'negligible' framing the abstract relies on; but the alternative (a referee discovering the spread independently in Table 2) is worse for credibility.

quote: Finally, we find less evidence for bias among working papers (Table B9). This finding is consistent with publication bias in the traditional sense, in which editors or referees prefer certain results
issue: On a generous reading this passage is a model of intellectual honesty: the authors report a result that could have been quietly shelved (working papers showing less evidence of bias would seem, naively, to undercut the 'p-hacking is the dominant mechanism' framing they adopt via Brodeur et al. 2023), and instead they offer a coherent alternative interpretation (editors/referees as the bias channel rather than authors' own specification search) AND immediately flag the limitation that undercuts over-reading it ('our sample of working papers is small, resulting in low statistical power; moreover, five techniques still find evidence of bias'). That said, a careful referee would note that this single finding sits in tension with the paper's chosen framing throughout (which leans on the Brodeur et al. claim that 'the latter [p-hacking] drives most distortion' to justify treating publication bias and p-hacking as observationally equivalent) -- if editorial/referee-stage bias is live in the working-paper-vs-published contrast, that is a different mechanism than the within-author p-hacking story the paper's broad definition is built to subsume, and the paper does not fully reconcile the two.
proposed_fix: Add one clause connecting this working-paper finding back to the introduction's footnote on the Brodeur et al. (2023) p-hacking-vs-publication-bias distinction -- e.g., noting explicitly that the working-paper contrast is suggestive of an editorial-stage channel that the paper's broad 'publication bias' umbrella is designed to accommodate rather than separate out, so the two threads are visibly reconciled rather than left as parallel observations.
risk_of_fix: Very low -- a connective sentence that ties together two already-reported observations; minimal risk of introducing error since no new claim or number is added.

location.section: 3 Publication Bias / Table 2 Panel C and Appendix robustness tables
location.table: Table 2, Panel C ('First-stage robust F-stat Observations' row, value 4,180)

issue: ABSENCE: the paper reports a first-stage robust F-statistic of 4,180 for the baseline MAIVE specification (Table 2, Panel C) -- a number so large it would normally foreclose any weak-instrument concern outright, which is a genuine point in the defense's favor.
