However, the paper never states this explicitly in prose (no sentence reads, e.g., 'the first-stage F-statistic of 4,180 indicates the instrument is far from weak'), nor does it report or discuss the corresponding first-stage F-statistics for the robustness-table variants (expanded dataset, non-winsorized data, working papers, preferred-estimates subset) where sample sizes shrink substantially and instrument strength could plausibly weaken. A rigorous reader is left to notice the strong baseline F-stat by combing the table rather than being walked through why instrument strength is not a live concern -- and left wondering whether it remains strong in the smaller subsamples where the IV machinery is also deployed.
proposed_fix: Add one sentence in the main text explicitly citing the first-stage F-statistic (4,180) as evidence the instrument is strong in the baseline specification, and ensure the corresponding F-statistics are populated and briefly discussed for each robustness variant in the Appendix tables -- this converts an already-favorable number buried in a table into an explicit rebuttal of the weak-instrument concern that the rival seat would otherwise be positioned to raise.
risk_of_fix: Very low -- if the F-statistics for the robustness variants are already computed (likely, given they would be a routine IV diagnostic), this is purely a presentation fix with no risk of altering any substantive conclusion; the only failure mode is if a robustness-variant F-statistic turns out to be weak, in which case surfacing it would (correctly) invite scrutiny the authors should welcome rather than avoid.

location.paragraph: paragraph beginning 'Nevertheless, all the models mentioned so far assume...'

quote: test of the Andrews-Kasy model, shown in Table B10 in the Appendix, suggests that in our case estimates are indeed correlated with standard errors even in the absence of publication bias, we prefer the MAIVE approach (available also as a web app at easymeta.org). MAIVE suggests strong publication bias and negligible mean effect beyond the bias.
issue: The paper designates MAIVE as its 'preferred' bias-correction estimator — the one that effectively anchors the headline 'negligible/close to zero' framing — on the strength of a single auxiliary diagnostic: a specification test of the Andrews-Kasy model (Table B10) that finds a nonzero correlation between (transformed) estimates and standard errors net of estimated publication probability. That single test is used to (a) indict the uncorrelation assumption underlying the linear meta-regression AND the AK selection model itself, and (b) simultaneously promote MAIVE to 'preferred' status. But the test result is a double-edged sword the paper does not turn on itself: if the AK-weighted residual correlation is large enough to disqualify AK and the linear techniques, the same finding (real, non-publication-bias correlation between estimates and standard errors driven by 'method choices,' as the paper itself says two sentences earlier) equally threatens MAIVE's own identifying exclusion restriction — MAIVE's instrument (inverse sqrt of degrees of freedom) is admitted by the authors to be 'correlated with the standard error by definition,' and degrees of freedom is plausibly one of exactly the 'method choices' (sample size, clustering, fixed effects, control sets) that the Table B10 test is diagnosing as a contaminant. The paper never runs an analogous over-identification or falsification test on the MAIVE instrument itself; it merely asserts the instrument 'can be expected to be less related to method choices' (a hedge: 'can be expected,' not demonstrated). One specification test is thus made to do triple duty — disqualify the linear baseline, disqualify (implicitly) the AK selection model the paper elsewhere calls the most rigorously founded technique, and crown MAIVE — without any test of MAIVE's own exclusion restriction.
proposed_fix: Either (a) report a direct exogeneity/falsification check on the MAIVE instrument itself (e.g., test whether the inverse-sqrt-df instrument correlates with the same set of method-choice moderators — clustering, fixed effects, control-variable counts — that the paper elsewhere collects as the 48 contextual factors), and show the residual correlation is materially smaller than the AK-model residual that disqualified the rival technique; or (b) reframe the preference for MAIVE as one input among several converging corrections rather than as a single-test-justified 'preferred' choice, explicitly noting that the same diagnostic logic that disqualifies AK/linear models has not been, but in principle could be, applied to MAIVE.
risk_of_fix: Running the proposed falsification test could show the MAIVE instrument is itself correlated with method-choice moderators (degrees of freedom is mechanically larger for studies with more controls, larger samples, or different clustering schemes), which would undercut the very headline correction the authors prefer — a result the authors may be reluctant to surface. A purely rhetorical reframing (option b) risks looking like it weakens the paper's central correction without adding new evidence either way.

logical-validity.reason: Quote: 'literature...does not provide evidence of large unconditional effects.' Central claim clearly stated.

location.paragraph: paragraph beginning 'The two assumptions mentioned above are commonly used...'

quote: A solution is to use the inverse of the square root of the number of degrees of freedom as an instrument for the standard error (Irsova et al., 2025). Such an instrument is correlated with the standard error by the definition of the latter and can be expected to be less related to method choices.
issue: The exclusion-restriction argument for the MAIVE instrument is asserted, not established, and is internally in tension with the paper's own three-part taxonomy of endogeneity sources two sentences earlier (measurement error, reverse causality via 'changes in clustering,' and 'unobserved heterogeneity, because some method choices may systematically influence both estimates and standard errors'). Degrees of freedom is mechanically determined by sample size and the number of estimated parameters — i.e., precisely by 'method choices' such as the inclusion of fixed effects, control variables, clustering structure, and subsample restrictions. The instrument (inverse sqrt of df) is therefore a function of the same method-design choices the paper just identified as a third source of endogeneity contaminating the standard error. The claim that the instrument 'can be expected to be less related to method choices' is a plausibility assertion with a hedge ('can be expected'), not a demonstrated exclusion restriction, and no falsification test, placebo, or over-identification check is reported to support it.
proposed_fix: Add an explicit test of whether the instrument (inverse sqrt of df) correlates with the very method-choice variables the paper itself collects (e.g., whether a study uses fixed effects, clustering, particular estimators, or particular control sets — several of the 48 coded contextual factors are exactly this kind of method choice). If the correlation is small, report it as direct support for excludability; if it is not small, the instrument's validity — and hence the 'preferred' designation — needs to be reconsidered or qualified.
risk_of_fix: If the requested correlation turns out to be non-negligible, the authors would need to either drop MAIVE as 'preferred' or substantially soften the headline 'negligible effect' framing that currently leans on it — a non-trivial reframing of the paper's central message that the authors may resist undertaking mid-review.

logical-validity.reason: Quote: 'people focus on the rewards instead of the work' (Rusz et al. 2020). Distraction mechanism cited.

issue: The quantitative results in Table 2 undercut the prose's framing of MAIVE as simply joining a chorus of techniques that 'corroborate' a negligible effect. MAIVE's reported 'effect beyond bias' coefficient is 0.0181 — larger than three of the five nonlinear techniques the paper showcases as 'robust evidence that the mean corrected incentive-performance effect is negligible' (Top10 = 0.0105, Andrews-Kasy = 0.00143, Kink = 0.00718) and roughly comparable to the simple OLS linear estimate (0.0195) the paper treats as the naively-biased baseline. MAIVE's 'publication bias' coefficient of 0.892 is also far larger than the AK model's analogous parameter (P = 0.309) and sits in the same range as the linear OLS slope (0.854) the paper says suffers from endogeneity. In other words, on the numbers actually reported, MAIVE looks more like the linear/OLS baseline the paper says is unreliable than like the nonlinear battery it is grouped with rhetorically — yet the prose folds it seamlessly into 'MAIVE suggests strong publication bias and negligible mean effect beyond the bias,' eliding that its point estimate is 2-13x larger than several of the techniques used moments earlier to establish 'negligible.'
proposed_fix: In the prose discussing Table 2, explicitly compare MAIVE's point estimate (0.0181) to the range produced by the nonlinear battery (0.0014-0.039) and acknowledge that MAIVE sits toward the upper, not the lower, end of that range — closer to the 'biased' linear estimates than to AK or Kink. State plainly whether 0.0181 is still classified as 'negligible' under the Doucouliagos (2011) thresholds the paper uses elsewhere, and if so, note how close it is to the threshold (analogous to the care taken with the 0.07 lab+loss-framing borderline case).
risk_of_fix: Drawing attention to the spread of point estimates across the 'preferred' and 'corroborating' techniques could visibly weaken the rhetorical unity of the 'battery all agrees' framing that currently does a lot of persuasive work in Section 3 — a fix that is honest but costs the paper some of its current narrative force.

logical-validity.reason: Paper analyzes interactions (appeal, task type, performance measure, framing, etc.) in Table 1 and Figure 4.

location.paragraph: paragraph beginning 'The fourth technique in Panel B of Table 2 is the selected model by Andrews & Kasy (2019)...'

quote: This technique has arguably the most rigorous foundations, and has been shown to perform relatively well both in simulations (Hong & Reed, 2021) and in comparisons of metaanalyses and pre-registered replications (Kvarven et al., 2019).
issue: The paper praises the Andrews-Kasy selection model as having 'arguably the most rigorous foundations' and citing favorable simulation and replication-comparison evidence (Hong & Reed 2021; Kvarven et al. 2019), then — two paragraphs later — uses a single specification test built on that very model's assumptions (Table B10, following Kranz & Putz 2022) to demote it in favor of MAIVE. This creates an unexamined tension: either the AK model's foundations are rigorous enough that its own diagnostic test should be taken at face value (in which case the paper should explain why a model it just called the most rigorously founded one fails its own specification check in this application, and what that implies for trusting the same model's weights when computing the Table B10 statistic itself — a logical circularity, since the test uses AK-estimated publication probabilities to weight the correlation it then uses to indict the uncorrelation assumption AK relies on), or the foundations are not as decisive as claimed and the earlier praise oversells the technique the paper is about to set aside. The manuscript does not address this tension.
proposed_fix: Add a sentence acknowledging the apparent tension directly: that the specification test used to motivate preferring MAIVE is itself constructed using AK-model-implied weights, and that this creates a degree of circularity the reader should be aware of — then explain why the authors nonetheless trust the diagnostic (e.g., because the diagnostic's qualitative conclusion — nonzero residual correlation — is robust to alternative weighting schemes, if that is true and can be shown).
risk_of_fix: If the diagnostic's conclusion is in fact sensitive to the AK weighting scheme used to construct it, surfacing this would further destabilize the case for preferring MAIVE over AK — a genuinely awkward position for the authors, but one better disclosed than left implicit.

location.paragraph: paragraph beginning 'Nevertheless, all the models mentioned so far assume...' (the three-source endogeneity taxonomy and the immediately following instrument proposal)

issue: The paper enumerates three sources of endogeneity that contaminate the linear meta-regression's standard-error regressor — measurement error, reverse causality (e.g., via clustering choices), and unobserved heterogeneity from method choices — and then immediately proposes MAIVE's degrees-of-freedom-based instrument as 'a solution.' But the manuscript never explains, for any of these three specific sources, why the chosen instrument is immune to it. In particular, source two ('reverse causality, because some researchers may, intentionally or not, manipulate the standard error... for example, by changes in clustering') maps directly onto degrees of freedom: clustering choices mechanically change the effective degrees of freedom used in significance tests, which is exactly the quantity the instrument is built from. The paper is silent on whether (and why) an instrument constructed from degrees of freedom escapes a contamination channel ('changes in clustering') that the paper itself names as operating through degrees-of-freedom-adjacent statistics.
proposed_fix: Add an explicit, source-by-source discussion mapping the instrument against each of the three named endogeneity channels — in particular addressing whether 'changes in clustering' (named explicitly as a contamination channel for the standard error) also contaminates the degrees-of-freedom-based instrument, since clustering choices directly determine the effective degrees of freedom reported and used in significance testing.
risk_of_fix: This is substantially the authors' own methodological judgment call about an estimator from their own prior work (Havranek et al. 2024; Irsova et al. 2025); a reviewer-proposed resolution risks putting words in the authors' mouths about a technical point that requires their own derivation or simulation evidence to settle properly.

logical-validity.reason: Quote: 'Only three studies overlap between our meta-analysis and that of Kim et al.' Minimal overlap noted.

quote: 5Another, more technical source of endogeneity is the transformation to standardized coefficients such as
issue: Footnote 5 begins to flag 'another, more technical source of endogeneity... the transformation to standardized coefficients such as [partial correlations]' but the footnote's content is interrupted by a page break in the extracted text and the substantive explanation appears to resume only as a fragment later ('partial correlations, which introduces a mechanical correlation between estimates and standard errors... MAIVE accounts for this problem as well'). The paper asserts that 'MAIVE accounts for this problem as well' but never shows how — there is no derivation, citation to a specific result, or even a sentence explaining the mechanism by which MAIVE's instrument neutralizes the mechanical correlation introduced by the PCC transformation itself. This is a load-bearing claim (a fourth, self-identified source of endogeneity specific to this paper's metric choice) asserted without support immediately before MAIVE is crowned 'preferred.'
proposed_fix: Expand footnote 5 (or move it into the main text given its substantive importance) to explain, in at least outline form, the mechanism by which the PCC transformation introduces a 'mechanical correlation between estimates and standard errors' and precisely how the MAIVE instrument breaks that mechanical link rather than merely asserting that it 'accounts for this problem as well.'
risk_of_fix: None of substance — this is a clarity/completeness gap whose remedy (spelling out an argument the authors evidently already have in mind) carries essentially no risk of introducing error, only the cost of additional length in an already dense methods section.

quote: Following Kranz & Putz (2022), the table shows, for various subsets of the literature, the correlation coefficient between the logarithm of the absolute value of the estimated inverse elasticity and the logarithm of the corresponding standard error, weighted by the inverse publication probability estimated by the Andrews & Kasy (2019) model. If the assumptions of the model hold, the correlation is zero.
issue: Table B10's specification test — the sole piece of evidence cited to justify preferring MAIVE — is itself a fairly indirect diagnostic: it reports a correlation between the log absolute value of an 'estimated inverse elasticity' and the log of the standard error, weighted by AK-model-implied inverse publication probabilities, and interprets a nonzero correlation as evidence that 'estimates are indeed correlated with standard errors even in the absence of publication bias.' This inferential chain runs through (a) a log-transformed re-expression of the PCC as an 'inverse elasticity' not otherwise used or defined in the main text, (b) AK-model-estimated weights (creating the circularity noted in F4), and (c) an implicit assumption that any residual correlation surviving AK-reweighting must be attributable to non-publication-bias sources rather than, e.g., AK model misspecification or weight-estimation noise (note the test's own reported correlation estimates carry wide bootstrapped confidence intervals, e.g. 0.647 [0.567, 0.668] for the baseline). The paper treats a positive point estimate from this multi-step, assumption-laden diagnostic as sufficient grounds to overturn the uncorrelation assumption and re-rank its entire preferred-method hierarchy, without discussing alternative interpretations of the same test result.
proposed_fix: Discuss, in the main text where Table B10 is invoked to justify the MAIVE preference, the alternative interpretations of a nonzero residual correlation in this test (AK misspecification, sampling noise in the AK weight estimates, the 'inverse elasticity' transformation's own properties) and explain why the authors read it specifically as evidence of estimate-standard-error correlation 'in the absence of publication bias' rather than as evidence against the AK model's own functional-form assumptions.
risk_of_fix: Engaging with alternative readings of the Table B10 result honestly could weaken the single strongest piece of stated justification for the MAIVE preference, forcing the authors to either find independent corroborating evidence or relax the confidence with which MAIVE is elevated to 'preferred' status.

quote: Notably, none of the psychology metaanalyses correct for publication bias.
issue: This is the paper's single sharpest claimed methodological gap relative to the rival literature -- it is the seat's own justifying quote for why this meta-analysis is needed -- yet it is a categorical claim about the contents of at least nine cited works (Wiersma 1992; Cameron & Pierce 1994; Deci et al. 1999; Cameron 2001; Cerasoli et al. 2014; Jenkins et al. 1998; Condly et al. 2003; Weibel et al. 2010; Garbers & Konradt 2014; Kim et al. 2022) stated flatly with no hedge, footnote, or per-study substantiation. Nothing in the surrounding text shows how each of these nine-plus studies was checked for the absence of a bias correction (vs., say, simply predating the methods this paper uses). Because web-grounding of cited works was not performed in this review, the claim cannot be checked against the originals from the manuscript text alone.
why_it_matters: The 'no prior bias correction in psychology' gap is the rhetorical fulcrum on which the paper's contribution claim (C-005/C-007, 'we correct the literature for publication bias... we focus on experimental economics... existing meta-analyses have concentrated primarily or exclusively on psychology') turns. If even one or two of the nine cited psychology meta-analyses did attempt some form of bias correction or sensitivity check (a live possibility for the more recent Cerasoli et al. 2014 or Kim et al. 2022), the blanket 'none' becomes an overclaim that a referee familiar with that literature would flag immediately, weakening the paper's framing of its own novelty.
proposed_fix: Either (a) add a brief substantiating clause or footnote for the 'none correct for publication bias' claim -- e.g., naming the specific check each cited study lacks (funnel plot, Egger's test, trim-and-fill, selection model) -- or (b) soften to a hedged form such as 'to our knowledge, none of the psychology meta-analyses we review formally correct for publication bias using the techniques we employ here', which preserves the contribution claim while not asserting an unverified universal negative about nine separate studies.
risk_of_fix: Over-hedging risks diluting a genuinely strong and probably-true contribution claim into mush; if the authors in fact already verified this (most likely, given their evident command of the bias-correction literature), a clumsy hedge could make the paper look less authoritative than it is. The fix should add precision, not retreat from a defensible claim.

quote: their analysis relies heavily on laboratory experiments, which account for 83% of the estimates and dominate the psychology literature. Only three studies overlap between our meta-analysis and that of Kim et al. (2022).
issue: This sentence does double duty: it reports a specific compositional statistic about a single rival study (83% of Kim et al.'s estimates are lab-based) and then, in the same breath, generalizes that lab experiments 'dominate the psychology literature' as a whole -- a much broader claim about an entire field's evidence base that a single 69-study, 82-effect-size meta-analysis cannot, by itself, establish. The 83% figure and the three-study overlap figure are themselves claims about the contents of Kim et al. (2022) that this paper's text does not show being independently re-derived (e.g., by re-coding Kim et al.'s included studies), so they read as taken on faith from the cited source.
why_it_matters: This passage is the paper's explanation for why a major rival psychology meta-analysis reaches the opposite substantive conclusion (a positive mean effect) -- i.e., it is the move that lets the authors dismiss a directly conflicting finding rather than engage with it. If the 83% or three-study figures are imprecise, or if 'dominate the psychology literature' overgeneralizes from one sample to a field, the explanation for the economics/psychology divergence -- a central interpretive pillar of the paper (see C-011, C-024) -- would rest on a shakier foundation than the confident, single-sentence dismissal suggests.
proposed_fix: Separate the two claims: keep the specific, presumably-verifiable statistic about Kim et al.'s sample composition and study overlap, and either substantiate the broader 'dominate the psychology literature' claim with an independent citation/statistic about the psychology literature as a whole (e.g., a share of lab vs. field studies across the cited psychology meta-analyses) or rephrase it as a claim specifically about Kim et al.'s sample ('...which dominates their sample') rather than the field at large.
risk_of_fix: Narrowing the claim to 'their sample' rather than 'the psychology literature' could be read as weakening the authors' explanation for the economics/psychology gap, inviting the question of whether the divergence is therefore less well understood than the original phrasing implied -- the fix should be paired with the existing, more defensible point that lab experiments are rare in this paper's own (economics) data (19%, C-010), which does the explanatory work without needing the broader generalization.

issue: Garbers & Konradt (2014) is cited only once, bundled into a list of five 'meta-analyses' on 'the overall effect of financial incentives on performance' (Jenkins et al. 1998; Condly et al. 2003; Weibel et al. 2010; Garbers & Konradt 2014; Kim et al. 2022), with no individual characterization of its findings, sample, or relationship to this paper's own sample -- unlike Weibel et al. (2010) and Kim et al. (2022), each of which receives a dedicated paragraph-level discussion (study counts, share from economics, overlap with this paper's sample, theoretical stance). Yet its reference-list title -- 'The effect of financial incentives on performance: A quantitative review of individual and team-based financial incentives' -- describes a quantitative review on precisely this paper's topic (financial incentives -> performance), arguably closer to this paper's exact subject than either Weibel et al. (intrinsic-motivation crowding in the public sector) or even some of the psychology-crowding-out papers that get more discussion.
why_it_matters: The seat's jurisdiction is whether the literature positioning is complete and whether 'any relevant prior work is missing or mischaracterized.' A quantitative review whose title maps almost one-to-one onto this paper's research question is treated as a one-line list entry while less topically-proximate studies (Weibel et al., the crowding-out papers) get sustained engagement. A reader cannot tell from the text whether Garbers & Konradt's findings align with, contradict, or are simply superseded by this paper's results, nor whether any of its included studies overlap with this paper's 88-study sample -- the same kind of overlap check the authors performed for Kim et al. (2022) ('Only three studies overlap...').
proposed_fix: Add one or two sentences characterizing Garbers & Konradt (2014) -- its scope (individual vs. team-based incentives), headline finding, and (if feasible) its overlap with this paper's sample -- at the same level of detail given to Weibel et al. and Kim et al., or explicitly state why it does not warrant the same treatment (e.g., narrower scope, superseded by a later review).
risk_of_fix: Minimal; the main risk is scope creep -- adding detailed treatment of every listed citation could bloat an already-dense introduction. The fix should be selective, reserved for citations whose titles suggest the closest topical proximity to the paper's own question.

quote: Again, the findings are mixed, but Weibel et al. (2010), who report a negative effect, remain the most frequently cited in the literature.
issue: The paper twice uses 'most frequently cited' as the criterion for which of several 'mixed' findings deserves headline attention -- once for Deci et al. (1999) on crowding-out, and again here for Weibel et al. (2010) on the overall incentive-performance effect. Citation frequency is a measure of a paper's prominence/influence in the field, not of its methodological quality, sample representativeness, or correctness -- criteria this paper itself elsewhere insists matter enormously (it spends most of its own length arguing that frequently-replicated, intuitively-appealing positive findings are often publication-bias artifacts). Selecting the comparison benchmark by citation count risks importing exactly the popularity-driven selection the paper otherwise critiques.
why_it_matters: Weibel et al. (2010) is then used as the specific foil for the paper's motivation-crowding discussion ('exactly as reported by Weibel et al. 2010'), so the choice of which prior finding to engage with substantively is not cosmetic -- it shapes which theoretical claim the paper tests itself against. If a less-cited but more methodologically comparable or more recent study reached a different conclusion, omitting it because it is 'less frequently cited' would be a selection criterion in tension with the paper's own publication-bias argument (that influential, intuitive findings are often the ones inflated by selective reporting).
proposed_fix: Replace or supplement the citation-count justification with a substantive one -- e.g., note that Weibel et al. (2010) is selected as the foil because it most explicitly operationalizes the motivation-crowding prediction this paper goes on to test, rather than (or in addition to) because it is most cited.
risk_of_fix: Low; this is a wording-level fix that does not require new analysis. The only risk is that, if citation frequency genuinely was the authors' intended (and defensible) criterion for choosing a representative 'consensus view' to contrast against, recasting it as a substantive choice could overstate how deliberately the foil was selected.

quote: These studies highlight the role of publication bias in experimental economics, as well as systematic variation in results based on experimental design.
issue: Imai et al. (2021), Brown et al. (2024), and Matousek et al. (2022) -- the three studies the paper calls 'closely related to our analysis' and groups as 'modern meta-analyses in experimental economics' -- are each given only a one-clause topic tag (present bias / loss aversion / individual discount rates) and then collectively credited, in a single follow-on sentence, with 'highlight[ing] the role of publication bias... as well as systematic variation in results based on experimental design.' No specific finding, technique, or number from any of the three is reported, so a reader cannot tell which of the three actually demonstrates which point, whether their bias-correction approaches resemble or differ from this paper's battery, or how this paper's contribution goes beyond what they already showed for their respective topics.
why_it_matters: These are explicitly flagged as the paper's closest methodological relatives (one of them, Matousek et al. 2022, is later credited as the direct source of this paper's 'preferred vs. non-preferred' classification method -- C-035/S-004), so a thin, undifferentiated group characterization in the literature-positioning paragraph leaves the reader unable to assess how this paper's methodological contribution (the bias-correction battery, the BMA exercise) differs from -- or merely repeats, in a new topical domain -- what these three sibling studies already established for present bias, loss aversion, and discount rates respectively.
proposed_fix: Expand the sentence into two or three, attributing the 'publication bias' and 'systematic variation by design' findings to the specific study (or studies) that actually demonstrated them, and briefly noting any methodological continuity (e.g., that the 'preferred estimate' classification follows Matousek et al. 2022, as is in fact stated later in Section 2) so the reader sees the lineage explicitly in the literature review rather than only encountering it in passing in the data section.
risk_of_fix: Minimal; mainly a length/balance tradeoff against an already information-dense introduction. Care should be taken not to duplicate the more detailed methodological attribution that already appears later (Section 2's citation of Matousek et al. 2022 for the preferred/non-preferred classification).

location.paragraph: robustness-checks summary paragraph beginning 'In the Appendix we provide several robustness checks'

quote: Fourth, we account for potential interdependence of reported estimates (Table B8). Our results do not change substantially if we consider just one estimate per study or one estimate per experiment.
issue: The paper offers the one-estimate-per-study/one-estimate-per-experiment exercise as the dependence-robustness check for its baseline headline result (the PCC-based, 1,252-estimate, '~0.03 corrected mean' finding). But Table B8's own regression notes state the dependent variable is Cohen's d, not the partial correlation coefficient ('Results of regression Dis = D0 + SE(Dis) + is, where Dis denotes Cohen's d coefficient'), and its observation counts (2,193 / 1,785 / 567) match the pooled/expanded Cohen's-d sample described elsewhere in the paper, not the 1,252-estimate baseline PCC sample that produces the headline '0.03' number. In other words, the check cited as evidence that the within-study/within-experiment dependence structure does not drive the baseline headline result is actually run on a different effect-size metric and a different (larger, robustness-only) sample -- it cannot, by construction, demonstrate that the baseline PCC headline survives one-estimate-per-study/-experiment subsetting, because no such subsetting of the baseline PCC sample is shown anywhere.
proposed_fix: Either (a) add and report the one-estimate-per-study / one-estimate-per-experiment robustness regressions on the actual baseline PCC sample (1,252 estimates, the sample that produces the headline 0.03/'close to zero' result) so the dependence check directly speaks to the headline, or (b) if Table B8 is intentionally run on the expanded Cohen's-d sample for power/coverage reasons, revise the prose so it no longer reads as direct evidence that 'our results' (i.e., the baseline headline) survive the dependence check -- explicitly state which sample and metric the check covers and why that licenses inference back to the baseline headline.
risk_of_fix: Re-running the dependence check on the smaller baseline PCC sample could reduce statistical power (fewer clusters per cell when collapsing 1,252 estimates to one-per-study/-experiment), potentially widening confidence intervals enough to flip significance -- which is exactly the scenario this finding warns could be hiding behind the current mismatch, so authors should be prepared for that outcome rather than treat the rewrite as cosmetic.

logical-validity.reason: Quote: 'mean...seem to be positive...for more recent studies. These studies are often conducted in a lab.' Directly stated.

location.paragraph: robustness-checks summary paragraph beginning 'In the Appendix we provide several robustness checks'

quote: Second, we analyze the expanded dataset, which is based on Cohen's d (Table B4). Here, evidence is even stronger for publication bias, and the corrected mean effect is close to zero.
issue: The text claims the expanded-dataset check shows publication-bias evidence 'even stronger' than baseline, citing only Table B4 (Cohen's d). But the companion Table B5 -- the expanded dataset expressed in the paper's own preferred PCC metric, arguably the more relevant comparison to the headline -- shows the p-uniform* endogeneity-robust technique finding essentially zero evidence of bias (publication-bias test statistic L = 0.008, p = 0.931, against a null of no bias), the opposite of 'even stronger.' The summary sentence cherry-picks the metric (Cohen's d) that supports 'stronger' bias and is silent about the PCC version of the same expanded-data check, which directly undercuts that characterization for one of the two endogeneity-robust techniques the paper otherwise treats as its most credible bias tests.
proposed_fix: Revise the expanded-dataset robustness summary to acknowledge that results diverge by metric: report and discuss Table B5 (PCC) alongside Table B4 (Cohen's d), and qualify the 'even stronger' claim to note that the endogeneity-robust p-uniform* test on the PCC version of the expanded data fails to reject the no-bias null (p = 0.93), while other techniques still detect bias.
risk_of_fix: Adding this caveat could read as weakening the paper's central publication-bias case; a careful rewrite needs to explain why the PCC/p-uniform* null result in the expanded sample does not undermine the baseline finding (e.g., power loss from averaging to study level) without appearing to suppress an inconvenient result.

quote: Third, we run the publication bias tests on the raw, non-winsorized dataset. For the baseline dataset (Table B6), we lose statistical significance in some specifications, but most of them are consistent with the baseline case, with our preferred MAIVE model giving almost identical results.
issue: The phrase 'we lose statistical significance in some specifications' is the paper's own admission that the headline publication-bias finding is sensitive to a basic, defensible choice (winsorizing vs. raw data), yet the prose neither names which specifications lose significance nor discusses what that pattern implies for the robustness of the headline. A reader is left to reverse-engineer from Table B6 which of the five linear and five nonlinear models flip; the prose's own framing -- 'lose... but most... consistent' -- concedes a non-trivial minority of specifications do not replicate, without telling the reader whether those are the more or less defensible specifications (e.g., OLS vs. fixed effects vs. precision-weighted), which matters because a specification-curve critique would ask precisely whether the surviving specifications are the theoretically preferred ones or merely the more numerous ones.
proposed_fix: Name explicitly which non-winsorized specifications lose significance (and why, e.g., outlier sensitivity in the OLS/precision-weighted columns versus the FE/BE/Study columns), and state whether the pattern of where significance survives correlates with the specifications the authors consider most credible -- rather than the generic 'most of them are consistent.'
risk_of_fix: Spelling out exactly which specifications fail could draw more referee attention to the fragility than the current vague phrasing, but suppressing the detail is itself the more serious problem a skeptical referee would flag; the fix is the right call even though it raises the salience of the fragility.

quote: In a similar vein, focusing on estimates emphasized by the authors of the primary studies (Panel C of Table B8) also yields substantial publication bias and a small corrected mean effect.
issue: This sentence reuses the 'preferred estimates' robustness framing that elsewhere (Section 2 / Table 1) is anchored to the baseline PCC sample's 396 'preferred' vs. 856 'non-preferred' split (1,252 total). But Panel C of Table B8 -- the panel this sentence cites -- reports N = 567 with Cohen's d as the dependent variable (per the table's own regression notes, inherited from the same Dis = D0 + SE(Dis) note that defines the whole table), i.e., a 'preferred' subsample of the expanded/Cohen's-d pool, not the baseline PCC 'preferred' subsample (396 estimates) that Table 1 and the main text describe. The reader is given no signal that 'preferred estimates' here means something different from 'preferred estimates' three pages earlier, creating a false sense that the same 396-estimate preferred-PCC subsample has been re-tested for dependence robustness when it has not.
proposed_fix: Disambiguate the two 'preferred estimates' subsamples by name (e.g., 'baseline-preferred (N=396, PCC)' vs. 'expanded-preferred (N=567, Cohen's d)') wherever both appear, and either add the missing baseline-PCC-preferred dependence check or clarify that Panel C's 567-estimate check is offered only as a complementary, not equivalent, robustness exercise.
risk_of_fix: Renaming/clarifying the subsamples is low-risk presentationally, but if the authors discover upon re-running that the baseline-PCC-preferred subsample (396 estimates) does not replicate the dependence-robustness pattern, the fix would surface a substantive gap rather than merely a labeling one.

quote: Finally, we find less evidence for bias among working papers (Table B9). This finding is consistent with publication bias in the traditional sense, in which editors or referees prefer certain results
issue: The working-paper subsample (408 estimates, 19 studies) is the one specification where the headline publication-bias story changes direction -- 'less evidence for bias' -- and the authors immediately supply a post hoc explanatory story (editors/referees as the bias source rather than p-hacking) for why the pattern flips there. But this is precisely the kind of 'where significance appears/disappears across checks' pattern a specification-curve critique flags as concerning: a result that weakens in exactly the subsample most plausibly driven by a different selection mechanism (no peer review filter) is consistent with either the authors' preferred story (editorial bias) or with the alternative that the working-paper sample is simply underpowered and noisy (which the authors concede in the same breath: 'our sample of working papers is small, resulting in low statistical power'). The paper does not test which of these two accounts is correct, yet uses the pattern to corroborate its bias-mechanism narrative.
proposed_fix: Either drop the editorial-bias interpretive gloss for the working-paper result (since the authors themselves note the sample is underpowered and cannot adjudicate between 'less bias' and 'too noisy to detect bias'), or explicitly flag the interpretation as speculative and offer the underpowered-sample explanation with equal weight.
risk_of_fix: Minimal -- softening an over-interpreted secondary result to an explicitly tentative one cannot make a true claim false.

quote: we obtain small and statistically insignificant effects in all cases, again with the borderline exception of lab experiments and framing as a loss (0.07)
issue: The paper's single positive headline finding -- the lab+loss-framing PCC of ~0.07 -- is repeatedly described by the authors themselves as sitting exactly 'on the threshold between a negligible and small effect' (per Doucouliagos 2011 guidelines), i.e., a hairline classification call rather than a robustly 'small' effect. From a specification-curve standpoint, a finding whose qualitative label (negligible vs. small, significant vs. not) hinges on which side of a guideline threshold a single point estimate with a reported 95% CI of (0.01, 0.14) happens to fall is fragile by construction: small perturbations to the bias-correction choice, the moderator set, or the implied-context computation (zero SE, preferred=1, sample-max year/impact factor/citations) could easily move the point estimate across that line. The robustness section never re-derives this specific implied-context number under the alternative bias-correction techniques (e.g., Andrews-Kasy, p-uniform*, non-winsorized data) that the paper otherwise uses to stress-test the overall mean -- the lab+loss cell is shown only once, from the MAIVE-anchored BMA pipeline.
proposed_fix: Recompute the lab+loss-framing implied estimate (and its CI) under at least one alternative bias-correction anchor (e.g., Andrews-Kasy or p-uniform*, both already run in the main battery) and report whether the 'borderline small' classification survives; if it does not, the abstract's framing of this cell as the paper's one robust positive exception needs to be softened accordingly.
risk_of_fix: Recomputing under alternative anchors could either confirm the result (strengthening the paper) or show it is anchor-dependent (requiring the authors to walk back their one positive headline claim) -- the latter outcome is uncomfortable but is exactly the test a skeptical referee would run, so deferring it only delays the same scrutiny to peer review.
